a-living-night-sky-underground-the-waito.context_blurb:
Beneath the green sheep country of New Zealand's North Island lies Waitomo, a maze of limestone caves. Visitors climb into a boat, the lamps go out, and the roof of a black grotto turns into a sky full of tiny blue-green stars. Every one of those stars is alive, and Māori guides have shown this underground heaven to travellers for well over a century.

The lights are glowworms, the glowing larvae of a small fungus gnat, which cling to the cave roof by the thousand and shine to lure insect prey toward them. In the dark their points of light look exactly like a starry night, and in a normal year about half a million people come to see them.

Nobody dug these caves. Waitomo is karst country: rainwater carrying a trace of acid from the air seeped down into the limestone and slowly dissolved it, leaving caves, sinkholes and underground rivers behind. The limestone itself formed on the sea floor about 30 million years ago, and its walls are still studded with fossil corals and seashells.

The boat follows the Waitomo Stream into the Glowworm Grotto, and the guides allow no talking and no torches. The glowworms are easily disturbed: loud voices or a flash of light make their glow dim and fade away, so only darkness and silence keep the living ceiling bright.

Māori living nearby had long known the black opening of this cave and stayed out of it. In Māori tradition the cave mouth marked an entrance into the underworld, so no one went inside. Then, in December 1887, the local chief Tāne Tinorau and Fred Mace, an English surveyor, lashed flax stems into a raft and poled in by candlelight, following the stream where it vanishes underground.

Within two years Tāne and his wife Huti were leading paying visitors through by candlelight, one of the earliest tourist ventures run by Māori. The government later took over the caves and ran them for most of a century, but in 1989 it handed them back to the descendants of Tāne and Huti, who own and run them today.

A species that lives naturally in one region and nowhere else is called endemic, and Arachnocampa luminosa is endemic to New Zealand: it shines in these caves and the country's wet forests and in no other land on Earth. Tasmanian caves such as Marakoopa glow too, but with different species that have never made it across the sea to New Zealand.

a-volcano-is-born-new-land-in-a-human-li.context_blurb:
Most volcanoes have stood in the same places for thousands of years. Every so often, though, the ground splits open somewhere new and a volcano is born where none stood before. Within living memory people have watched it happen in a Mexican cornfield, in the cold sea off Iceland and in the waters of Indonesia and Japan, and saw fresh land appear within a single lifetime.

In February 1943 the farmer Dionisio Pulido saw his cornfield near Paricutin crack open and begin spitting ash, and within one day the new cone stood about 50 metres high, as tall as a fifteen-story building. It kept growing until 1952, when it stopped at 424 metres and fell silent for good.

For nine years Paricutin's lava crept outward and buried the town of San Juan Parangaricutiro under hardened black rock, and only the bell tower of its church still rises above the flow. Pilgrims still walk out across the old lava to the church's surviving altar.

The lava moved too slowly to catch anyone, yet Paricutin still took three lives: its towering ash cloud built up a huge charge of static electricity, and the victims were struck by lightning.

From 1963 to 1967 an undersea eruption built a new island, Surtsey, just south of Iceland. Scientists closed it to everyone but researchers so they could watch how life reaches bare land. When a tomato plant sprouted there from waste a researcher had buried, the scientists pulled it up at once, because the island had to stay pristine for the experiment to mean anything. The first plant to arrive on its own, sea rocket, took root in 1965.

In Indonesia's Sunda Strait, the volcano Krakatoa blew itself apart in 1883. In Indonesian anak means child, so the young volcano that climbed out of the same water is Anak Krakatau, the Child of Krakatoa. It rose for good above the waves in 1930 and has been growing, collapsing and rebuilding ever since.

About 1,000 kilometres south of Tokyo, a 2013 eruption raised a small new islet beside the island of Nishinoshima. Flow after flow welded the two together until the island was some twenty times its old size. Every acre of cooling lava, and the sea around it, became new Japanese territory, so each eruption quite literally made Japan bigger.

abu-simbel.context_blurb:
In the far south of Egypt, close to the border with Sudan, four stone giants sit side by side on the bank of a desert lake. They are the pharaoh Ramesses II, and behind them lie his two temples at Abu Simbel, carved about 3,200 years ago to proclaim his glory. In the 1960s the whole site nearly vanished under water, and the world joined forces to save it.

Abu Simbel was not built from blocks at all: Ramesses II's workers chiselled the facade, the halls and the four seated colossi, each about 20 metres high, straight out of a living sandstone cliff. The whole temple is really one carved mountain.

When Egypt built the Aswan High Dam across the Nile, the waters of Lake Nasser began rising toward the temples, so between 1964 and 1968 an international rescue team sawed Abu Simbel into 1,036 numbered blocks and moved them uphill to higher ground. The Great Temple took 807 of those blocks and the small temple beside it 235.

That small temple Ramesses dedicated to Hathor, the goddess of love, joy and music, in honour of his queen Nefertari. It is one of very few temples where a queen's statues on the front stand as tall as the pharaoh's, and inside she appears as Hathor herself.

The rescuers had to decide what to restore and what to leave alone. In ancient times an earthquake had knocked the head and shoulders off the second of the four colossi. The engineers chose not to repair it, and they set the broken pieces back on the ground at the statue's feet, exactly where they had fallen.

The team lifted the temples 65 metres up the cliff and set them about 208 metres back from the water. They fitted the huge carved blocks together again to within about 5 millimetres, so tightly that the seams are almost invisible. That precision mattered, because the temple was built to catch the sun.

Twice a year, around 22 February and 22 October, the dawn sun shines down a corridor some 60 metres long and falls on three of the gods seated at its far end, including Ramesses himself, while the fourth, Ptah, a god linked with the underworld, stays in darkness. Many believe the ancient builders planned this on purpose.

The modern rebuilders came remarkably close to the original, but it is widely reported that the sunlit mornings used to fall around 21 February and 21 October, so the move shifted them by about a day. Even with modern machines, nobody could quite match 3,200-year-old astronomy.

ajanta-caves.context_blurb:
In the hills of Maharashtra in western India, a cliff curves like a giant horseshoe above the Waghora River. Along its face open about thirty Buddhist halls and monasteries, painted with princes, queens, elephants and dancers. Monks worked here for centuries, then left, and the jungle hid Ajanta from the outside world for over a thousand years.

At Ajanta no one laid a single brick or block: the monks cut every pillar, doorway and ceiling out of the living basalt of the gorge, so each finished hall is a hollow inside solid rock.

The walls inside burst with ochre and deep blue, still glowing after about 1,500 years, and no other place on Earth keeps so much ancient Indian painting. Almost every scene illustrates a Jataka tale, a story of one of the Buddha's earlier lives, when he was born as a prince, an animal or even a great six-tusked elephant, and each life teaches a virtue such as patience or generosity.

The best-loved painting of all, in Cave 1, shows Padmapani, whose name means the lotus-bearer: a gentle crowned prince holding a blue lotus, a form of the bodhisattva of compassion. It is the most reproduced image of Ajanta.

Ajanta's caves come in two kinds: viharas, square monastery halls ringed with small cells where monks lived, and chaityas, tall prayer halls built around a domed stupa so pilgrims could walk around it. Five of the caves are chaityas, and the oldest of them all, Cave 10, is one.

In April 1819 a British officer, Captain John Smith of the Madras army, was out hunting a tiger in the hills when he glimpsed a dark opening, and a village boy guided him into the painted halls. Smith scratched his own name and the date onto a pillar in Cave 10, across a painting 1,500 years old, and the graffiti can still be read.

The first small caves date to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE. After some six silent centuries, the Vakataka emperor Harishena sponsored the grandest halls and finest murals around 460 to 480 CE. His dynasty collapsed soon after his death, the carvers put down their tools mid-work, and so many of the later caves were never finished, with roughed-out pillars, blank walls and figures only half freed from the rock.

akrotiri-and-the-thera-eruption-santorin.context_blurb:
Santorini, the island the ancient Greeks called Thera, rises from the Aegean Sea as a broken ring of cliffs around a deep blue lagoon. The ring is what remains of a volcano that exploded around 1600 BCE in one of the largest eruptions of the last ten thousand years. Under its ash lies a Bronze Age town so well kept that its houses still stand.

The great bay of Santorini is a caldera, the basin left behind when a volcano empties its underground chamber of melted rock and its summit collapses into the gap. The sea poured in, and today ships sail into a drowned basin about 12 by 7 kilometres across, ringed by cliffs nearly 300 metres high.

Archaeologists digging through the ash found Akrotiri, a town of the Minoan world with paved lanes, clay drainpipes and houses two and three storeys tall. People call it a second Pompeii. Yet Akrotiri was buried about 1,600 years before Pompeii, deep in the Bronze Age, which makes its standing walls all the more astonishing.

Pompeii's ash held thousands of victims. Akrotiri held almost none. The best explanation is that warning earthquakes shook the town before the blast, and its people fled in good order, taking their valuables with them. That is why the excavators found the houses nearly empty.

In 1999 they made one rare find: a small golden ibex, or wild goat, tucked in a wooden box inside a clay chest beside a heap of animal horns, the only object of solid gold in the entire town. One forgotten treasure only confirms how carefully everyone else packed.

The people left their art behind. In 1970 excavators uncovered the Spring Fresco, with swallows darting over red lilies on volcanic rock, and it became famous as the first Aegean wall painting ever found still in place on the wall where it was painted. Earlier finds had been pieced together from fallen fragments.

The eruption wiped out a rich and advanced society in a blast of sea and ash. Some scholars have wondered whether a distant memory of Thera's fate inspired Plato's story of Atlantis, the island civilization swallowed by the sea, but the link remains a guess that no one has proved.

aksum.context_blurb:
High in the mountains of northern Ethiopia stands Aksum, once the capital of one of the great empires of the ancient world. From about the 1st to the 7th century CE its kings commanded the trade of the Red Sea, and in the 4th century the kingdom became one of the first anywhere to adopt Christianity. It is still a holy city, and its skyline is a field of giant standing stones.

Those stones are stelae, each a single block of rock. Aksum's carvers shaped each stele to look like a tall tower-house of the kind Aksumites really lived in, with rows of false windows on every storey and a false door at the foot, carved right down to the lock. The Obelisk of Aksum shows nine storeys; the Great Stele shows thirteen. But the stones were grave markers, not homes: each tall stele stood over the underground burial chamber of an Aksumite king, so the whole field is really a royal cemetery.

The most famous of them made a long journey. In 1937, during Mussolini's occupation of Ethiopia, Italian troops cut the 24-metre, 160-tonne Obelisk of Aksum into three sections and hauled it to Rome, where it stood for about 68 years. In April 2005 Italy finally sent it home by air, its three sections flown one at a time in a giant Antonov An-124, one of the largest cargo planes in the world. The obelisk stood again in Aksum in 2008.

The stones came from Gobedra Hill, about 4 kilometres west of the city. To free a block, workers cut a groove in the rock, hammered in wooden wedges and soaked them with water, and as the wood swelled it split the stone away. Teams of labourers then dragged the giants to the burial field. The Great Stele, about 33 metres long and 520 tonnes, may be the biggest single stone anyone has ever tried to stand on end, and scholars believe it toppled and shattered during the effort to raise it. It still lies where it fell, broken across a crushed tomb.

Aksum grew rich carrying goods between Africa's interior and the Roman world: its Red Sea ports sent out ivory, tortoiseshell and gold, and took in silk and spices carried from as far away as India. Around 270 AD King Endybis began striking Aksum's own coins in gold, silver and bronze, the classic sign of a kingdom that answered to no greater ruler. Very few kingdoms of that age, and hardly any in Africa, did the same.

Those coins later recorded a turning point. In King Ezana's reign, around 340 AD, the old pagan crescent and disc vanished from Aksum's coins and a Christian cross took their place, making them some of the first coins in the world to carry one. Ezana's reign also saw the first church dedicated to St Mary of Zion rise in Aksum. For centuries an Ethiopian ruler could be crowned as true emperor only here, at Aksum, in a ceremony bound to that church.

Next to St Mary of Zion is a small chapel kept under constant guard. Ethiopian Orthodox tradition holds that it keeps the holy Ark of the Covenant, the sacred chest of the Hebrew Bible, brought from Jerusalem by Prince Menelik I, son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Only a single guardian monk may see it; he is appointed for life and may never leave the grounds. The claim is a matter of faith that no one has proved or disproved.

alexandria.context_blurb:
On the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, where the Nile delta meets the sea, Alexander the Great founded a city in 331 BC and gave it his own name. Under the Greek kings who ruled Egypt after him, Alexandria became the grandest city of its age, home to a famous lighthouse, a legendary library and scholars from across the Mediterranean.

Alexander's architect Dinocrates laid the city out on a grid of broad straight avenues, but Alexander himself marched off to conquer Persia within months and never came back to see it completed.

The city's great lighthouse, the Pharos, counted among the ancient world's Seven Wonders, a tower perhaps 100 to 130 metres tall with a fire burning at the top through the night. By day a great polished mirror at its summit caught the sun and flashed it out to sea, and sailors were said to see the gleam almost 47 kilometres from shore.

The Library of Alexandria, founded around 285 BC under Ptolemy II, aimed at nothing less than one copy of every book that existed anywhere. It gathered tens of thousands of papyrus scrolls, though ancient guesses at the total range wildly.

A city that grand earned a legend about its birth. Plutarch tells that Alexander, with no chalk to hand, marked out the city walls on the dark soil with pale barley meal. Then great flocks of birds flew down and gobbled up the whole outline, frightening Alexander until his seers declared it a good omen: the city would one day feed people from many nations.

The Pharos stood for many centuries, until earthquakes in 956, 1303 and 1323 brought it crashing down. Around 1480 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built his fortress on the same rocky point, salvaging the fallen stones of the ruined Pharos itself.

The hunt for books grew ruthless. Ships entering the harbour were searched, and any scrolls on board were carried off to be copied out by the Library's scribes. The Library held on to the originals and handed the owners fresh copies instead, and it catalogued its prizes as the books of the ships.

The city hides wonders underground as well. Under the modern city lie the burial halls of Kom el Shoqafa, the Mound of Shards, carved out in Roman times and then forgotten for over a millennium. They came to light by accident in 1900, when a donkey suddenly dropped through the ground into the buried shaft. Inside, three cultures meet: the Egyptian god Anubis wears Roman armour beside a carving of a Greek myth.

Alexandria's most famous scholar measured the planet itself. Around 240 BC Eratosthenes, chief of the Library, heard that at noon on the longest day the sun shone straight down a well at Syene, far to the south, while in Alexandria an upright pole still cast a shadow. That shadow showed the sun about 7.2 degrees off overhead, one fiftieth of a full circle, so Eratosthenes multiplied the distance from Syene to Alexandria by fifty and worked out the whole circumference of the Earth, within about one percent of the true figure.

amritsar-the-golden-temple-in-its-sacred.context_blurb:
In the city of Amritsar in Punjab, northern India, a shrine of gold seems to float on a square lake. It is the Harmandir Sahib, the holiest place of the Sikh faith, a religion born in the 15th century that teaches the equality of all people before one God. Pilgrims of every faith and every station walk its marble pavements day and night.

The shrine stands on an island in the middle of the pool. Only one way leads to it: a narrow marble causeway, the Guru's Bridge, about 200 feet long and 21 feet wide, so every visitor, rich or poor, crosses the water by the same path.

At sunrise the whole pool seems to catch fire. The upper storeys, dome and towers are covered in real gold, about 400 kilograms of gold leaf laid on around 1830 by order of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and the low sun strikes that gold and pours its glow across the water. That gleam gave the shrine its English name, the Golden Temple.

The pool is the Amrit Sarovar, the pool of nectar, which gave Amritsar its name, and the faithful revere its water as amrit, a nectar believed to heal both body and soul. Guru Ram Das, the fourth Sikh Guru, had the great tank finished around 1577, and pilgrims still wade in at dawn to drink from it.

The fifth Guru, Arjan, built the shrine low, with steps leading down to its entrance where other faiths climbed up to theirs, and he is remembered as explaining that God dwells with the humble, those who bow, rather than with the proud. He gave it a door on each of its four sides, open to every caste and faith from every direction.

Beside the temple runs the langar, often called the largest free kitchen in the world. About 500 volunteers cook around 50,000 meals on an ordinary day and over 100,000 on festivals, and a machine turns out some 200,000 flatbreads. To show that everyone at the meal is equal, princes and paupers alike sit down together on the floor to eat.

amsterdam-the-city-on-piles-below-the-se.context_blurb:
Amsterdam, the capital of the Netherlands, rises from soggy ground where great rivers meet the North Sea. Much of it lies below sea level and would flood without the dams, dikes and pumps the Dutch have built for centuries. In the 17th century, the Dutch Golden Age, this swampy port became the hub of one of the richest trading empires on Earth.

In the 1600s the city dug its famous rings of canals, and today about 1,200 bridges span more than 100 kilometres of waterways, stitching together some 90 islands, a denser web of bridges than Venice has.

The city's very name tells how it began. Around 1270 fishermen settled where a small tidal river, the Amstel, met the sea, but storm tides kept flooding the marsh. So they built a dam across the river's mouth, and the town behind it took its name from that barrier: Amstel-dam, Amsterdam. Dam Square, at the heart of the city, still marks the spot.

Building on peat and clay takes a trick. The stone Royal Palace stands on 13,659 whole tree trunks, fir and spruce shipped from Scandinavia, driven about 12 metres down through the mud to a firm layer of sand. The poet Constantijn Huygens called the building the world's Eighth Wonder. It opened as the city hall in 1655 and became a royal palace only in 1808.

Water seeps up endlessly into land that lies below the sea, and much of central Amsterdam sits about 2 metres under it. For centuries the Dutch kept their country dry with windmills, whose sails turned a giant screw or scoop-wheel that lifted the water up and over the dikes. Electric and diesel pumping stations took over the work only later.

After a flood in 1675, Mayor Johannes Hudde set a fixed water mark that grew into the Amsterdam Ordnance Datum, the zero level from which heights are still measured across much of Western Europe.

Walk the canals and the tall, narrow houses seem to lean, many of them forward over the street. The stairs inside were too steep and tight for furniture, so people hauled goods up the outside with a hook on a beam at the top of the gable. Builders tipped the fronts forward on purpose, a style called op de vlucht, so that loads swinging up on the hoist would not bang against the bricks. A house leaning sideways is another story: its wooden piles are usually rotting, and it really is sinking.

angel-falls.context_blurb:
Deep in the rainforest of southeastern Venezuela, a ribbon of water leaps from the rim of a flat-topped mountain and falls almost a kilometre into the jungle. This is Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world, so remote that most visitors reach it by small plane and dugout canoe. The mountain it pours from is one of the strangest landforms in the world.

The falls drop 979 metres in all, 807 of them in one unbroken plunge, and in the dry season so much of the water shreds into spray that it drifts away as mist before ever reaching the valley floor.

The cliff belongs to Auyán-tepui, and tepui is the Pemón people's word for these sheer-walled table mountains, which they call the houses of the gods. Their flat summits are islands in the sky, cut off from the forest below by cliffs on every side.

Whatever water survives the fall runs off as the Churún River, then into the Carrao, and at last into the Orinoco, one of the great rivers of South America.

The English name honours Jimmie Angel, an American pilot, but the Pemón had always known the falls. Their own name, Kerepakupai Merú, means waterfall of the deepest place, and Venezuela made it the official name in 2009.

Angel first flew past the falls in 1933 while hunting for a rumoured bed of gold. In 1937 he set his plane down on the summit, only for its wheels to sink into soft bog and would not budge, and Angel and his party needed 11 days to scramble down on foot. His plane, El Río Caroní, sat abandoned on top of the mountain for 33 years, until in 1970 the Venezuelan Air Force lifted it off in pieces by helicopter. Restored, it now stands at the airport in Ciudad Bolívar.

Lonely summits like these fired the imagination of writers. Arthur Conan Doyle, the creator of Sherlock Holmes, read explorers' accounts of Mount Roraima, a neighbouring tepui, and in 1912 published The Lost World, in which dinosaurs survive on a remote plateau.

The tepuis are made of layered sandstone and quartzite about 1.7 to 1.9 billion years old, some of the most ancient rock at the surface of the planet, resting on the Guiana Shield. They are the last hard stumps of one great sandstone highland that once stretched unbroken across the region, until erosion wore away everything between them.

angkor-siem-reap.context_blurb:
Just north of the Cambodian town of Siem Reap, temple towers rise out of the jungle across a wide green plain. This was Angkor, the capital of the Khmer Empire, which ruled much of Southeast Asia from about the 9th to the 15th century. Its builders shaped stone into a picture of the universe, and its engineers tamed the monsoon itself.

The grandest temple of all is Angkor Wat. Its five towers, shaped like lotus buds, are the white silhouette in the middle of Cambodia's national flag, where Angkor Wat has appeared since 1863. King Suryavarman II raised it about 900 years ago across some 400 acres, and Guinness World Records lists it as the biggest religious monument anywhere on Earth, though not the biggest building of every kind.

Angkor Wat is a temple-mountain: its five towers stand for the five peaks of Mount Meru, the home of the gods at the centre of the Hindu and Buddhist universe, and its moat for the sea that encircles that mountain. Nearly every Khmer temple faces the sunrise, but Angkor Wat's main gate faces west, toward sunset and the land of the dead, and scholars such as George Coedès read that as a sign that Suryavarman II also built it as his own funerary temple.

Most of Angkor's temples were cleared of jungle and pieced back together, but not Ta Prohm. Twentieth-century restorers deliberately left Ta Prohm the way explorers had first seen it, with giant strangler figs pouring over its walls, so visitors could see a temple still locked in the forest's embrace. The roots hold the stones together and pry them apart at the same time, and a film shot there in 2001 earned it the nickname the Tomb Raider temple. A stone inscription King Jayavarman VII set up there in 1186 lists nearly 80,000 people assigned to serve this one temple-monastery.

Jayavarman's own state temple, the Bayon, carries about 200 colossal human faces on its towers, calm and faintly smiling, which may show the bodhisattva of compassion, the king himself, or both. Smaller and finer is Banteay Srei, the Citadel of the Women, a pink sandstone jewel consecrated in 967 and built by a royal courtier rather than a king, with carving as delicate as a goldsmith's work. In 1923 the future French writer André Malraux was arrested for stealing statues from it.

Angkor Wat's eastern gallery holds a carving some 49 metres long of a famous Hindu myth. Gods and demons wrap the serpent Vasuki round a mountain and pull it back and forth to churn the Sea of Milk. They are churning for amrita, the elixir of immortality.

Angkor's real power lay in water. The monsoon brings floods of rain, then months of drought. To bridge the dry season, the Khmer dug a baray, a giant rectangular reservoir, to store monsoon water and feed the rice fields. The West Baray, about 7.8 by 2.1 kilometres, has a small island temple at its centre.

For centuries people imagined Angkor as a scatter of temples lost in the trees. Then archaeologists flew over the forest bouncing laser beams off the ground and clocking each echo, a method called LiDAR, to map the land beneath the canopy. The surveys revealed a planned grid of roads, canals and neighbourhoods stretching for miles, the remains of the largest city anywhere before the industrial age.

That city, perhaps 700,000 strong, emptied slowly through the 1300s and 1400s. Tree rings record years of severe drought and destructive floods as the climate shifted, and they wrecked the water-control network Angkor depended on, until people abandoned the city.

angkor-thom-and-the-bayon.context_blurb:
In the late 12th century the Khmer king Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom, a walled royal city in what is now Cambodia, ringed by a moat and entered through five tall gates. At its exact heart stands the Bayon, a crowded mountain of stone towers. Wherever a visitor stands, enormous carved faces seem to be watching.

More than 200 giant serene human faces still look out from the Bayon's towers in every direction, earning it the nickname the smile of Angkor. When the French writer Pierre Loti first saw them, he wrote that his blood curdled as one smile after another appeared above him.

The lower galleries show something rare in ancient art: ordinary life. Women sell fish in a market, two people play chess, and a woman gives birth. In one crowded scene, bookies take bets as men lean in to watch a cockfight.

No inscription says whose faces crown the towers. Scholars most often identify them as the bodhisattva of compassion, Avalokiteshvara, though many think they also show Jayavarman VII himself, his gaze reaching every corner of his kingdom. The Bayon was the last great state temple raised at Angkor, and Jayavarman made it Mahayana Buddhist.

The five gate towers rise about 23 metres above the moat, each crowned with four faces looking north, south, east and west. At their feet stands Airavata, the three-headed elephant of the god Indra, with Indra on its back and its trunks reaching down to pluck lotus flowers.

Not every carving is myth. One long panel shows war canoes crammed with warriors ramming each other while fighters tumble into water full of fish and crocodiles. It records a real naval war between the Khmer and the Chams of Champa, fought on the Tonle Sap, the great lake at the heart of Cambodia. The Cham warriors can be picked out by their distinctive headgear.

The road to every gate crosses a causeway over the moat, lined with two rows of stone giants hauling on a vast serpent, like a tug-of-war. The bridge retells the Hindu story of churning the Ocean of Milk, in which gods and demons wind the serpent Vasuki round a mountain and pull it back and forth to win amrita, the elixir of immortality. There are 54 gods on one side and 54 demons on the other: the gods have calm oval faces, the demons bulging eyes and scowls.

angkor-wat.context_blurb:
On the plain north of Siem Reap in Cambodia stands Angkor Wat, built in the first half of the 12th century by the Khmer king Suryavarman II. It began as a vast temple-mountain to the Hindu god Vishnu and later became Buddhist. Its five towers rise above a moat so wide it looks like a lake, and monks have tended it ever since.

Angkor Wat has been the emblem of Cambodia since 1863, and its white silhouette sits at the very center of the national flag, on the broad red band between two blue ones.

The whole temple is a model of the universe. In Hindu belief Mount Meru rises at the centre of creation, and the towers of Angkor Wat are its peaks. The moat, 190 metres across and over 5 kilometres in circumference, stands for the primordial cosmic ocean that surrounds Meru at the edge of the world.

When the Khmer court moved away toward Phnom Penh in the 1400s, the jungle swallowed Angkor's other temples, but Buddhist monks never left Angkor Wat, and their unbroken care for some 800 years is a big reason it survived nearly whole.

A 49-metre gallery holds the most famous carving at Angkor, the Hindu myth of churning the Ocean of Milk, with 88 gods and 92 demons hauling on the serpent Vasuki as if in a giant tug-of-war. They are churning for amrita, the nectar of immortality, and in the story they start fighting over it the moment it appears. When the mountain they use as a churning stick starts sinking, Vishnu becomes a giant turtle, Kurma, and holds it up on his shell from the sea floor.

Angkor Wat breaks two rules. Almost every Khmer temple faces east, but this one faces west, the direction of sunset and of death in Hindu belief, and its wall carvings run anticlockwise, against the lucky direction. Those choices lead many scholars to conclude that Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat as a king's tomb, his own funerary temple. After he died he was called Paramavishnuloka, he who has gone to the supreme world of Vishnu.

The stone itself made a journey. All of the sandstone, between 5 and 10 million blocks, came from Phnom Kulen, a sacred plateau 40 to 50 kilometres to the northeast that the Khmer honoured as the birthplace of their empire, and the blocks were floated to the site on canals.

The Khmer also built for the monsoon, storing rain to water rice through the dry months. Their greatest reservoir is the West Baray, about 7.8 by 2.1 kilometres, dug by hand and still holding water after 900 years. It belonged to a grid of canals and moats that covered roughly 1,000 square kilometres.

Only the stone temples outlasted the jungle; the wooden city around them rotted away. In 2012 Damian Evans and his team hung a LIDAR scanner under a helicopter, firing laser pulses at the ground and timing their return to map the bare earth beneath the trees. In about 20 hours of flying they uncovered a lost city spread over some 1,000 square kilometres, home to perhaps 750,000 people or more.

Ancient cypress tree rings show why that city faded: two long megadroughts, in the mid-1300s and early 1400s, emptied its reservoirs, and the fierce rains that broke them clogged the canals with debris. The water system never recovered, and the court moved on.

antarctica.context_blurb:
Around the South Pole lies Antarctica, a whole continent buried under ice up to several kilometres thick. It is the coldest, driest and windiest place on Earth, and it has no permanent residents, just scientists rotating through a few dozen research stations. Under the ice lie lakes, trenches and secrets older than humanity.

Antarctica is the planet's greatest store of fresh water: its ice sheet holds about 90 percent of all the ice on Earth and roughly 70 percent of all fresh water. Yet it counts as the largest desert on Earth, because a desert is defined by how little moisture falls, not by heat, and the frozen interior gets only about 150 millimetres a year, less than the Sahara.

On 21 July 1983 the Soviet base Vostok, perched 3,488 metres up on the inland ice, logged minus 89.2 °C, the lowest natural air temperature ever recorded on the planet. That is more than 70 degrees colder than a home freezer.

No nation has ever been born here. Under the Antarctic Treaty of 1959, signed by twelve nations, every land claim was frozen and no country owns the continent, which is set aside for peace and science, with military bases, mining and nuclear weapons all banned.

The McMurdo Dry Valleys, about 4,500 square kilometres of bare rock and gravel, are the largest ice-free patch of Antarctica, and since the 1970s NASA has tested rovers and drills there because no place on Earth looks more like Mars. Nearby, a blood-red stain spills out of the end of Taylor Glacier, but Blood Falls is iron-rich salt water, sealed under the ice for one to two million years, which rusts the moment it meets the air. Robert Falcon Scott's men found it in 1911 and were unnerved by the sight.

Radar shows that the ice averages about 1.9 kilometres thick, and at its deepest, in the French-claimed sector of Terre Adélie, it reaches about 4,776 metres, nearly 3 miles, roughly 4.8 kilometres down to bedrock.

The ice hides whole lakes. Lake Vostok, as large as Lake Ontario, lies under some 4 kilometres of ice, and its liquid water has been cut off from sunlight and air for perhaps 15 to 25 million years. Scientists study it in the search for hardy microbes. On Ross Island, Mount Erebus, at 3,794 metres the most southerly active volcano in the world, has held a churning lake of molten lava in its crater ever since the early 1970s, and probably far longer. Its gas plume even carries off tiny amounts of gold vapour every day.

The ferocious winds have a name: katabatic winds, from a Greek word for descent, which form when heavy, frozen air on the high plateau slides downhill under its own weight and rushes toward the coast at up to 300 kilometres an hour.

The ice is so heavy that it has pressed the bedrock far below sea level, as low as 2,555 metres in the Bentley Subglacial Trench, and if the ice ever vanished, the land would slowly spring back up over thousands of years, a balancing act geologists call isostasy.

Antarctica was not always frozen. Fossil leaves of Glossopteris, a tree that flourished some 260 million years ago and more, have been found in South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica, the first clue that all these southern lands were once joined in the supercontinent Gondwana.

antarctica-the-windiest-coldest-place-on.context_blurb:
Antarctica's frozen interior regularly drops below minus 80 °C, and gales sweep down from its ice sheet to the coast almost every day. The ice is so cold and dry that cores drilled from it hold records of the climate stretching back more than 800,000 years. There are no cities and no permanent residents, only teams of scientists who come and go.

Guinness World Records names Commonwealth Bay, on the coast of East Antarctica, as the windiest spot on Earth, where freezing air pours off the high ice sheet almost without pause, so the average wind for the whole year is about 80 kilometres an hour and blizzards have topped 240.

The Australian explorer Douglas Mawson and his men built their hut at Cape Denison, on that bay, and wintered there in 1912, and in 1915 Mawson titled his book about the ordeal Home of the Blizzard, a name that has stuck to the place. His expedition had set up camp, without knowing it, on the windiest coast on Earth.

Inland the air is calmer but even colder. The record belongs to Vostok Station, a Russian base about 3,488 metres up on the East Antarctic ice sheet, where the air sank to minus 89.2 °C on 21 July 1983. Its height and its distance from any warming ocean, some 1,300 kilometres from the South Pole, explain the cold. Satellites have since spotted even colder patches of ice surface, but those are not air temperatures.

Beneath that same station lies Lake Vostok, the biggest of roughly 675 lakes hidden under Antarctica's ice: about 250 kilometres long and 50 wide, sealed under about 4 kilometres of ice for perhaps 15 million years. In February 2012 Russian scientists finished the longest ice core ever drilled and broke through to water no light had touched in millions of years.

The same katabatic winds that batter the coast sweep the McMurdo Dry Valleys bare of snow, leaving cold, rainless, nearly lifeless ground that NASA has long used as its closest stand-in on Earth for the surface of Mars.

The Transantarctic Mountains split the continent's ice in two. The far larger half is the East Antarctic Ice Sheet, and its melting alone would lift sea levels everywhere by some 60 metres. The smaller sheet lies to the west.

atalh-y-k.context_blurb:
On the plain of central Turkey stands a low mound called Çatalhöyük, the remains of one of the earliest towns ever found. People began building it around 7500 BCE, more than four thousand years before anyone raised Stonehenge. Thousands lived here in mud-brick houses packed so tightly together that the whole town worked like a honeycomb.

There were no streets and no front doors. The flat rooftops served as the town's lanes and meeting places, and each family entered its home from above, through a hole in the ceiling with a ladder leading down into the main room.

The dead stayed close to the living. A dead relative was folded up tightly, knees to chest, and buried beneath the floors and raised sleeping platforms inside the house, so every household slept above its own ancestors. Years later they sometimes dug up a skull, coated it in plaster and painted the face with red ochre to bring back the features of the dead.

About 8,600 years ago someone at Çatalhöyük painted a wall with a bird's-eye view of rows of houses and a twin-peaked mountain spouting fire behind them, and it is often called the oldest map in the world. The archaeologist Stephanie Meece offered a rival reading: the spotted shape everyone calls a volcano is really a leopard's spotted skin, hung above a geometric pattern. The argument is still open. Geologists have since shown that the nearby volcano Hasan Dağ really did erupt during those centuries, which keeps the map idea alive without proving it.

athens.context_blurb:
Athens, in southern Greece, is one of the oldest cities on Earth that people have never stopped living in. In the 5th century BCE, in one brief, dazzling burst, it gave the world democracy, the tragedies of Aeschylus and Sophocles and the questions of Socrates. Above it all rises a rock crowned with marble temples that still draws every eye in the city.

That rock is the Acropolis, a name that means high city: a flat-topped crag of limestone about 70 metres above the streets, which Athenians crowned with their greatest temples.

The greatest of them is the Parthenon, built around 440 BC for the goddess Athena. Its name comes from one of Athena's titles, Parthenos, which means the maiden, since in myth she never married. The marble holds faint traces of iron that slowly react with air and sunlight, so instead of shining chalk-white the Parthenon glows a warm, golden honey colour, especially at dusk.

Below the rock lay the Agora, the gathering place, an open square of markets, law courts and shrines where Athenians traded and argued, and where Socrates buttonholed strangers with his questions.

On a low hill at the Agora's western edge stands the Temple of Hephaestus, god of the forge, built around 450 BC and never wrecked, so it keeps its roof and columns and is the most complete Greek temple anywhere.

The Parthenon hides a secret. Its architects, Iktinos and Kallikrates, made hardly a line in it truly straight. Each column swells gently near its middle and tilts a little inward, so far that the columns' lines would meet more than a kilometre overhead, and these deliberate curves fool the eye into seeing a temple that looks perfectly straight and alive. The marble floor even rises a few centimetres at its centre. All that marble, some 20,000 tons, came from Mount Pentelicus, which gave its name to fine white Pentelic marble, and teams hauled it about 19 kilometres to the city and up the rock.

On the smaller Erechtheion temple nearby, the roof of one porch rests on the heads of six marble women, the Caryatids. The weathered originals now stand indoors in the Acropolis Museum; Lord Elgin carried one off to the British Museum in London. Inside the Parthenon once stood the Athena Parthenos, a statue nearly 12 metres tall that Phidias made of gold and ivory laid over a wooden frame. The gold could be lifted off, and in time the statue was stripped and lost.

The city's democracy had its own sharp tool. Once a year Athenians could vote to banish one over-powerful man for ten years by scratching his name on a broken bit of pottery, an ostrakon, and from that word comes ostracism. Archaeologists have dug thousands of these shards from the Agora.

The Parthenon served as a temple, then a church, then a mosque, and stood almost whole for over 2,000 years. Then, on 26 September 1687, a Venetian army besieging the Ottomans on the Acropolis fired a mortar that struck the gunpowder the Ottoman soldiers had stored inside, and the blast tore off the roof and killed about 300 people.

auckland.context_blurb:
Auckland, New Zealand's biggest city, spreads across a narrow neck of land on the North Island with a harbour on either side. Look across its suburbs and green humps rise everywhere between the houses and parks. Each one tells the same fiery story, and the ground beneath the city is not finished yet.

Every one of those rounded hills, from Mount Eden to One Tree Hill, is a volcano, one of about fifty-three separate centres of the Auckland Volcanic Field, which can still erupt.

The city loves its water just as much. Aucklanders own more boats for their numbers than nearly any people on Earth, once about one boat for every three households, and in 1985 the city was officially named the City of Sails.

The youngest and biggest volcano of all is Rangitoto, a near-perfect cone that rose from the sea off the city around 1450 CE, and its lava makes up about 41 percent of everything the field has ever erupted. Its smooth, even outline is the backdrop to every harbour view.

People saw it happen. On the neighbouring island of Motutapu, archaeologists found human footprints pressed between layers of Rangitoto's ash, left by Māori who walked across the fresh ashfall. They are the clearest proof that the eruption happened in living memory.

Auckland's is a monogenetic field: each eruption builds one new volcano at a fresh spot, and once it cools, that cone never erupts again. Rangitoto is the lone exception, with two phases about fifty years apart. So geologists expect the next eruption to break out somewhere new, at a place no one can yet point to.

Long before Europeans arrived, Māori lived on this isthmus and fought for it, because its volcanic soil grew rich gardens of kumara and its two harbours brimmed with fish. They called the place Tāmaki Makaurau, which means Tāmaki desired by many.

ayutthaya.context_blurb:
For more than four hundred years Ayutthaya was the royal capital of Siam, the kingdom that became Thailand. Seventeenth-century European visitors compared its size and splendour to Paris and London. Then, in 1767, an invading army burned it, and its red-brick towers and broken Buddhas still stand in ruins on the central Thai plain.

King U-Thong founded Ayutthaya in 1350 on an island where three rivers meet, above the reach of the sea tides, so enemy warships could not sail up to its walls. Canals laced the city so thickly that European traders called it the Venice of the East.

The most photographed sight among the broken towers of Wat Mahathat is a stone Buddha's head held in the roots of a fig tree that slowly grew around it. No one knows exactly how the head came to rest there; by tradition it lay among the rubble as the temple crumbled, and the tree did the rest. Thais treat the spot as sacred.

At Wat Lokayasutharam a brick-and-plaster Buddha 42 metres long lies on his side, a pose that shows the moment of his death, as he passed into final Nirvana.

Three bell-shaped towers stand in a row at Wat Phra Si Sanphet, the royal chapel inside the old palace, and they hold the ashes of King Borommatrailokkanat and two of the kings who came after him. No monks ever lived there; it belonged to the king alone.

Around 1700, Ayutthaya may have held close to a million people, a bigger population than London's. Portuguese, Dutch, Chinese and Japanese merchants came to trade, and each foreign community lived in a district of its own strung along the riverbanks. The Japanese village held about a thousand people, and a Greek sailor, Constantine Phaulkon, rose to become one of King Narai's most powerful ministers.

The end came with the Burmese invasion of 1767. The Burmese soldiers who looted the city knocked the heads off the rows of stone Buddhas and stripped away their gold, so long galleries of headless statues still line the temples.

After a siege of fourteen months, the Siamese chose not to rebuild on the ashes, and instead founded a new capital downstream on the Chao Phraya River that grew into modern Bangkok. Ayutthaya was left as the ruins visitors walk through today, now a World Heritage Site.

baalbek.context_blurb:
In the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon stands Baalbek, where Roman builders raised one of the largest temple complexes in their empire. Its chief temple honoured Jupiter. The columns are giants, but what really amazes visitors is the platform underneath, built of stones so heavy that engineers still argue about how the Romans moved them.

Six columns of the Temple of Jupiter still stand, each about 20 metres high, the height of a six-story building, and nearly 2.5 metres thick, the largest temple columns anywhere in the Roman world. Once there were 54; earthquakes and stone-robbers brought the rest down.

Set into the temple's western wall more than 4 metres up are three blocks called the Trilithon, each over 19 metres long and weighing some 800 tonnes. They are joined so perfectly that even a knife blade will not slide into the seams between them. They rest on a row of smaller stones that each still weigh around 300 tonnes.

In the quarry just outside town lies an even bigger block of roughly 1,000 tonnes, shaped by Roman quarrymen and then abandoned. Local people call it Hajar al-Hibla, which means Stone of the Pregnant Woman, and folk tales say a pregnant woman, or a race of giants, once lifted it. In truth it simply never left the spot where the quarrymen cut it.

The Romans began the Temple of Jupiter around 16 BC. Archaeologists learned that it was finished around AD 60, under Nero, from a scrap of graffiti that a workman scratched on one of the topmost column drums. So the temple took about 75 years to build.

In 2014 a team from the German Archaeological Institute measured another stone in the quarry, about 19.6 metres long and 1,650 tonnes, the biggest block of stone people have cut anywhere on Earth. Flawed rock at one edge meant it might crack if anyone tried to shift it, so it was never dragged away from the spot where it was carved.

How the Romans moved the Trilithon is still not proved, but there is nothing mysterious about who did it: the blocks lie under a temple that Roman builders demonstrably raised. The engineer Jean-Pierre Adam calculated that about 512 men turning capstans, drums that wind in rope, and working pulley blocks could drag a stone of 557 tonnes.

babylon-and-the-ishtar-gate.context_blurb:
On the flat river plain of Mesopotamia, in today's Iraq, Babylon was for centuries the greatest city of the ancient Near East. In the 6th century BCE King Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt it in brilliant glazed brick, with a soaring temple-tower and a gate that blazed blue. Ever since, Babylon's name has stood for splendour and for pride.

Babylon rose on the Euphrates, which flowed straight through the heart of the city. Its ruins lie near the modern town of Hillah, about 85 kilometres south of Baghdad.

Around 575 BC Nebuchadnezzar raised the Ishtar Gate, honouring Babylon's goddess of love and war. Its bricks were glazed a deep, glowing blue to match lapis lazuli, the most treasured blue stone of its age, dug from distant mines in the mountains of Afghanistan. To face a whole gate in that colour announced Babylon's wealth to everyone who came near.

Golden beasts stride across that blue. The lions belonged to Ishtar and the wild bulls to the storm god. The strangest creature, the scaly dragon called the mushhushshu, was the sacred beast of Marduk, Babylon's supreme god. It is a patchwork monster, with a snake's scales and flickering tongue, a horned crest, a lion's front legs and, at the back, an eagle's talons. Its name means something like furious serpent.

The Babylonians said their city's name, Bab-ilim, meant gate of the gods, a fitting title for a city of temples. Modern scholars suspect that reading was laid over an older name nobody remembers, but for the ancients it stuck.

Nebuchadnezzar explained his choice in an inscription on the gate itself: he set the bulls and dragons there so that the people would look at them and marvel. Through the gate ran the Processional Way, lined with marching lions, and the Babylonians named it Aibur-shabu, a boast meaning that no enemy would ever get past. Each spring, at the New Year festival, priests carried the statue of Marduk down this road and out through the gate.

The Bible's Tower of Babel probably remembers a real building: Etemenanki, the giant stepped temple-tower of Marduk, whose name meant the foundation of heaven and earth. Alexander the Great ordered the crumbling tower pulled down so it could be rebuilt even grander, but he died in 323 BC before the work was done.

The gate itself made a long journey. The archaeologist Robert Koldewey dug up its shattered bricks between 1902 and 1914. They were shipped to Germany, and in 1930 the front gate was rebuilt indoors in Berlin's Pergamon Museum, where visitors walk through it today. Only the smaller front section fits; the original was a much larger double gate.

Koldewey noticed that the gate's lions and bulls were real animals, and in 1918 he wondered whether the dragon might be too, comparing it to an Iguanodon, a dinosaur known only from fossils. Most scholars think the mushhushshu was always a creature of myth.

Babylon's most famous wonder has never been found at all. Legend says Nebuchadnezzar built the Hanging Gardens for his homesick queen, Amytis, but no trace of them lies in Babylon's soil. Stephanie Dalley, a scholar at Oxford, believes the gardens were real but grew at Nineveh, built by the Assyrian king Sennacherib.

bagan.context_blurb:
On a wide bend of the Irrawaddy River in central Myanmar lies the plain of Bagan, once the religious capital of a medieval Burmese kingdom. From the 11th to the 13th century its kings and people covered the dry grassland with Buddhist temples. At dawn, as mist lifts and hot-air balloons drift overhead, spires poke above the trees as far as the eye can see.

Around 2,000 brick temples and pagodas still stand on the plain, about 2,200 in all, built by kings and nobles who believed each new temple earned merit for the next life. Balloons have carried visitors over them in the dry season since 1999.

Yet those survivors are only a remnant: at the height of the Pagan Kingdom, between 1044 and 1287, around 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries rose across the plain. Neglect, looting and earthquakes have thinned them ever since.

Bagan's best-loved shrine is the Ananda, a white temple with a golden spire finished in 1105 under King Kyansittha, where four gilded standing Buddhas, each about 9.5 metres tall, face north, south, east and west. Its spires were gilded afresh for the temple's 900th birthday in 1990.

The largest temple, the dark Dhammayangyi, has a grimmer story. King Narathu built it around 1167, and legend says he had seized the throne by murdering his father and his brother. Haunted by guilt, he demanded flawless brickwork, and the story goes that any mason was put to death if a needle could be slipped between two of his bricks. Historians treat the tale as folklore, but the joints really are famously tight.

The plain lies in earthquake country. In August 2016 a quake of magnitude 6.8 shook Bagan and damaged nearly 400 of its roughly 3,250 monuments in a single day. Quakes over the centuries are one reason so few of the original temples survive.

From the air the whole plain glows a warm rusty red, unlike the grey stone towers of Angkor or Borobudur. That is because almost every temple at Bagan is built of fired brick rather than carved stone.

baghdad.context_blurb:
Baghdad sits on the Tigris River in today's Iraq. The caliph al-Mansur founded it in 762 as the new capital of the vast Abbasid Empire, and for a few golden centuries it was the richest and most learned city on Earth, where scholars gathered the knowledge of Greece, Persia and India. Then, in 1258, came the Mongols.

Al-Mansur built his capital as a perfect circle, which he named the City of Peace, with his palace and great mosque at the exact centre and four gates facing the roads to distant cities. Some 100,000 workers built it, yet virtually nothing of the Round City survives.

The Greeks called the land around Baghdad Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers, because it lies between the Tigris and the Euphrates. The world's first cities, the first writing and the wheel all appeared there.

In the early 800s Caliph al-Ma'mun gathered scholars into the House of Wisdom, where they translated the works of Aristotle, Euclid and the physicians of Greece into Arabic. Legend says al-Ma'mun loved learning so much that he paid each translator the weight of his finished book in gold. Around 820 the mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title, al-jabr, gave us the word algebra, and his own name, written in Latin as Algoritmi, gave us algorithm. He also helped spread the Hindu-Arabic numerals, zero included, that we still use.

In 1258 the Mongol army of Hulagu Khan, grandson of the conqueror Genghis, sacked Baghdad and flung so many books into the Tigris that chroniclers said the river ran black with ink. Some modern historians doubt the story, but the libraries were gone. The Mongols wrapped the last Abbasid caliph in a carpet and trampled him with horses, because they would not spill royal blood on the ground.

Hardly a stone of the Abbasid golden age remains. One rare survivor is the Mustansiriya Madrasa, a college that Caliph al-Mustansir founded in 1227 beside the Tigris, old enough to have lived through the Mongol sack and among the oldest university buildings still standing. A modern Baghdad university took up its name in 1963.

bali-uluwatu-and-the-subak.context_blurb:
Bali is a small island just east of Java in Indonesia, and in a mostly Muslim country it remains overwhelmingly Hindu, with a faith and culture all its own. Temples crown its sea-cliffs and rocks, and inland, below smoking volcanoes, its hillsides step down in glittering terraces of flooded rice fields watered by a system more than a thousand years old.

On the island's southern cliffs stands the temple of Uluwatu, whose name joins two Balinese words, ulu for tip and watu for rock, and so means tip of the rock, the spot where Bali's land drops into the sea.

Hindu temples stand guard all around the coast, placed so that sailors and fishermen could see and honour them from the sea. Tanah Lot, on the southwest shore, perches on a lone rock, and its name means land in the sea. When the tide comes in, the sea closes all the way around the rock and cuts the temple off as an island, and visitors can walk out to it only after the water falls again.

When the sun goes down at Uluwatu, as many as 150 men sit shirtless in a ring by firelight and chant cak-cak-cak to retell the Ramayana epic. This dance, the Kecak, uses no musical instruments at all: the interlocking voices of the chorus do the work of a whole orchestra, with no drum, gong or string. The dancer Wayan Limbak shaped it in the 1930s with the German painter Walter Spies, building on an older trance ritual.

Inland, streams from the volcanoes are split among the fields by channels, little dams and shrines. For more than a thousand years Balinese farmers have shared it through the Subak, groups of growers who meet and decide together how the water is divided, and UNESCO named the Subak landscape a World Heritage Site in 2012. Each of Bali's roughly 1,559 subaks is led by an elected chief who sees that every farmer gets a fair share.

The soil is famously rich. Mount Agung, which towers 3,031 metres over the island, erupts from time to time and showers the countryside with ash, which weathers into some of the most fertile soil on Earth. The Balinese revere Agung as an earthly copy of Mount Meru, the cosmic mountain.

In the cool north, Lake Batur fills part of a caldera, a vast bowl about 10 by 13 kilometres left when a volcano's summit collapsed into its emptied chamber of molten rock. The active cone of Mount Batur stands inside the same bowl, and the lake, Bali's largest, feeds the rice terraces below.

The water-temples stand exactly where springs rise and channels fork, following Tri Hita Karana, the Balinese idea of harmony among people, nature and the divine.

bangkok.context_blurb:
Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, sprawls across the flat lowland where the Chao Phraya River meets the Gulf of Thailand. It grew from a riverside village into a city of about ten million, with glittering temples and floating markets in the old centre and skyscrapers beyond. It is built on mud, and it is slowly sinking.

Thais call their capital Krung Thep, City of Angels, the first words of a ceremonial name 168 letters long that Guinness lists as the longest place name on Earth. Foreign traders found the old village name, Bangkok, easier to say, so the rest of the world kept it.

In the 1800s the city was laced with canals called khlongs, and most people travelled by boat, so Western visitors nicknamed it the Venice of the East. Floating markets still sell fruit from boats, and the Chao Phraya remains the city's great watery highway.

Thailand's holiest image sits in the royal chapel of the Grand Palace. The Emerald Buddha is not emerald at all but a single block of deep-green jade, and emerald describes only its colour. Legend dates it to 43 BCE; scholars place the carving around the 15th century. For all its fame it is tiny, just 66 centimetres tall, set far above the crowds on a towering gilded altar. It owns three golden costumes, for the hot, rainy and cool seasons, and by custom only the King of Thailand, or a senior royal standing in for him, may climb up to change them.

Across the river rises Wat Arun, the Temple of Dawn, its central spire about 70 metres high and covered in millions of pieces of broken Chinese porcelain that arrived as ballast in the holds of trading ships. It is named for Aruna, the Hindu god of the dawn.

At Wat Pho lies a gilded Buddha 46 metres long and 15 metres high. Under its skin of gold leaf, the giant is made of brick and plaster. The soles of its feet, each 5 metres long, are inlaid with 108 panels of mother-of-pearl showing the sacred signs by which a Buddha is known. Wat Pho is also where traditional Thai massage was born and is still taught, whose healing lines are carved on stone tablets around the temple, and its graduates now work in 145 countries.

The city's name has humble roots. In 1782 King Rama I founded his new royal capital on an island in the river, around a village called Bang Makok. Makok is the olive-plum tree, so the village name meant place of olive plums. Rama I ringed the island with canals and called the royal district Rattanakosin, Jewel of Indra.

Bangkok stands on a delta, the low, flat, fan-shaped land a river builds where its current slows at the sea and drops its mud and sand. The Chao Phraya runs 372 kilometres to get here, and its delta barely rises above the sea, so a hard monsoon downpour easily floods the streets, which is why the old city was threaded with canals instead of roads.

barcelona-gaud-s-growing-basilica.context_blurb:
Barcelona, the great port of Catalonia on Spain's Mediterranean coast, is a city shaped by one man's imagination. Antoni Gaudí, a devout Catalan architect of the late 1800s and early 1900s, filled it with swooping houses, parks and churches that seem to have grown out of the sea or the forest. His masterpiece is a church still rising from its scaffolding.

That church is the Sagrada Família, whose first stone was laid on 19 March 1882, and it has been a working building site ever since, one of the longest construction projects in human history. Millions of visitors come each year to watch it climb.

Gaudí spent his final four decades on it, even living on the site and refusing other paid work, so the people of Barcelona called him God's Architect. In 1926 a tram struck him in the street, and he was buried in the crypt beneath his unfinished church, with less than a quarter of it built.

On 20 February 2026, exactly 144 years after work began, builders set the top arm of the cross on the central Tower of Jesus Christ, and at 172.5 metres the Sagrada Família passed Germany's Ulm Minster, the tallest church in the world since 1890.

Even so, Gaudí made the tower bow. He kept its summit a metre lower than the crest of Montjuïc, Barcelona's highest natural hill, because he believed nothing built by human hands should stand taller than what God had made.

Inside, the columns lean and branch as they rise. Gaudí designed the interior as a stone forest: the tree-like columns split into thinner shafts that hold up the roof from within, so the church needs none of the flying buttresses that prop up a Gothic cathedral from outside.

He found his curves by experiment. Gaudí hung tiny sacks of lead pellets on a net of strings, and each string sagged into a natural loop, a curve called a catenary. Then he flipped the sagging model upside down, because the same curve turned over becomes an arch in which stone only presses together and never pulls apart or cracks. He tested the method on the church of Colònia Güell and used it throughout the Sagrada Família.

The church stands in the Eixample, the district the engineer Ildefons Cerdà planned in 1859. From above, every block has its four corners cut off, turning each square into an octagon. Cerdà sliced those corners so that every crossing would open up, letting in more light and air, widening the view down each street and giving carriages room to turn.

batik-javas-wax-drawn-cloth.context_blurb:
Batik is the Indonesian art of painting cloth with wax and then dyeing it, and the island of Java is its traditional home. A single Javanese piece can take months, with layer after layer of waxing and dyeing building up dazzling patterns, and UNESCO counts Indonesian batik among the world's great cultural treasures. The secret of the whole craft is a simple trick.

The wax keeps the dye out: wherever it covers the cloth, the colour cannot soak in, so when the wax is removed the hidden lines show pale against the dyed background. The wax adds no colour of its own; it only guards the cloth.

The finest work is batik tulis, written batik, drawn with a canting, a pen-like tool: a little copper reservoir of melted wax that ends in a fine spout, fixed to a wooden handle. When the hot wax hardens and clogs the spout, the artisan often gives it a quick puff of breath to push the plug out and keep the line flowing.

Hand-drawing can take weeks for one cloth. In the 1800s workshops sped things up with the cap, a carved copper stamp pronounced chop, which presses a whole block of pattern onto the cloth at once.

When the dyeing is done, the cloth looks like a mess, its pattern buried under a crust of coloured wax. The last step, nglorod, boils the cloth in hot water, often with soda ash, until all the wax melts off and the design finally appears. With thick wax, this washing-out can take days.

Patterns could carry rank. In the royal courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta, the grandest designs were larangan, a word that means forbidden: they were reserved for the sultan and his relatives, and a commoner caught wearing one could be punished. The diagonal parang was the classic example; its largest form belonged to the reigning sultan alone.

Legend says Sultan Agung, the 17th-century king of Mataram, designed the parang during long meditation on the shore at Parangtritis, in the south of Java, watching hour after hour as the waves broke against the cliffs. Its name comes from a Javanese word for a slope or cliff, and its endless line of linked S-shapes stands for striving that never stops.

The same pattern also carries a warlike edge, like a sword hacking on and on. For that reason Javanese custom says a guest should not put on parang for a wedding, in case its fighting spirit stirs up quarrels between bride and groom. It is folk belief, but many still follow it.

beijing-the-imperial-capital.context_blurb:
Beijing has been China's capital for most of the last seven hundred years. At its heart lies a walled palace where emperors once ruled a quarter of humanity, and the whole old city was laid out as a model of cosmic order, gate after gate and courtyard after courtyard along one great north-south line. The imperial pattern can still be traced from the air.

That palace is the Forbidden City, built between 1406 and 1420 under the Ming emperor Yongle, the biggest and best-preserved palace complex in the world, with about 980 buildings and some 8,700 rooms across 72 hectares. Twenty-four emperors lived there, and ordinary people were kept outside its moat.

From any high point you could spot the emperor's buildings, because golden yellow roof tiles belonged to the throne alone, while ordinary roofs stayed grey. One grand exception is the great round prayer hall at the Temple of Heaven, roofed in deep blue to echo the sky.

Legend says the builders deliberately stopped half a room short of ten thousand, because a full ten thousand belonged only to the palace of the Jade Emperor in Heaven, and no earthly ruler dared equal the gods. A survey in 1973 actually counted about 8,700. Visitors enter through the Meridian Gate, about 38 metres high and crowned with five pavilions, and only the emperor himself could pass through its tall central archway.

That harvest prayer hall, a round wooden tower 38 metres high under three roofs, is held together entirely by interlocking brackets and slotted joints, without one nail. The hall standing today is a faithful rebuild after lightning burned the first one in 1889.

Around the palace wind the hutong, narrow grey lanes that date back to the 1200s, when the Mongol rulers of the Yuan dynasty made Beijing their capital. The word hutong comes from a Mongolian word for a water well, the shared heart of each little neighbourhood. The lanes are lined with courtyard houses joined wall to wall.

Northwest of the city lies the Summer Palace and its lake. In 1893 Cixi, the Empress Dowager, completed a two-storey boat on the lakeshore, complete with paddle-wheels, but it will never sail, because the Marble Boat is carved from stone. Kunming Lake itself, 2.2 square kilometres of water, was dug out by hand, and the workers heaped every basket of earth into Longevity Hill, which rises 60 metres beside it. Along the shore runs the Long Corridor, 728 metres of covered walkway with every crossbeam painted with a different scene, over 14,000 pictures in all.

At the Temple of Heaven, the smooth circular Echo Wall around the Imperial Vault of Heaven works as a whispering gallery: a soft whisper spoken close to its glazed brick slides along the curve and can be heard all the way round on the far side.

Palace roofs carry little processions of glazed beasts down their corner ridges, and a building's rank decided how many it could have, up to a legal limit of nine. Only the throne hall at the empire's ceremonial heart, Taihedian or Hall of Supreme Harmony, carries a tenth figure, a monkey-faced immortal called Hangshi.

The city's grandest monuments line up along the Central Axis, a ceremonial spine 7.8 kilometres long running from the Drum and Bell Towers in the north through the Forbidden City to the gate of Yongdingmen. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 2024.

bergen.context_blurb:
On Norway's rugged west coast, ringed by mountains on three sides with the open sea on the fourth, lies Bergen. In the Middle Ages it was Norway's biggest city and a key outpost of a powerful trading alliance. Today it is the starting point for journeys into some of the grandest scenery on Earth, and it is famous for its rain.

Along the old harbour on Vågen bay leans Bryggen, which simply means the wharf, a row of tall pointed wooden buildings painted red, brown and yellow that has become the emblem of the city.

For about four hundred years, from the mid-1300s until 1754, German merchants of the Hanseatic League ran a walled trading post behind those gables and controlled the trade in stockfish, Norway's dried cod. That fish fed much of Catholic Europe on its meatless fast days.

Boats from Bergen head into the fjords, valleys that Ice Age glaciers gouged far below sea level before the sea flooded in when the ice melted. Sognefjord, the longest and deepest of them, plunges 1,308 metres, and Bergen's place between it and Hardangerfjord has made it the gateway to the fjords.

Rain falls on about 240 days a year, some 2,250 millimetres in all, and Bergen is widely called Europe's rainiest city. The world record belongs to Mawsynram in India. Locals joke that a true Bergener never carries an umbrella; he simply tugs his hood up and lets the rain pass. The cause is orographic rainfall, from the Greek word for mountain: wet Atlantic winds hit the ring of mountains, rise, cool and drop their water on the town.

Ludvig Holberg, a playwright of the 1700s, gave Bergen its fond nickname, the city of seven mountains, to make it echo Rome, the famous city of seven hills. Bergeners still cheerfully argue about which seven peaks should count.

The League ran four big trading stations abroad, known as Kontors, in London, Bruges, Novgorod and Bergen. Only at Bergen do the medieval wharf buildings still stand, rebuilt again and again on their old footprints after fires, and in 1979 UNESCO listed Bryggen as the last surviving Kontor of the League.

bodh-gayas-bodhi-tree-and-the-traveling-.context_blurb:
In the eastern Indian state of Bihar, monks and pilgrims from all over Asia gather in silence around a single sacred fig tree. Buddhist tradition holds that here, in the 5th century BCE, a wandering seeker named Siddhartha Gautama sat in meditation until enlightenment dawned on him and he became the Buddha, the Awakened One. It is the holiest place in Buddhism.

The town is Bodh Gaya, on the bank of the Falgu River, a place that in the Buddha's own day was called Uruvela.

Around 250 BCE the emperor Ashoka, a champion of Buddhism, placed a polished stone slab beside the tree to mark where the Buddha sat, and it is called the Vajrasana, which means the Diamond Throne. Ashoka also built the first shrine on the spot.

The Mahabodhi Temple, a tower 55 metres high raised in the Gupta era about 1,500 years ago, is built almost entirely of brick, and it is one of the oldest brick buildings still standing in India. It became a World Heritage Site in 2002.

The tree has a family tree of its own. Around 288 BCE, the chronicles say, Ashoka's daughter Sanghamitta, who had become a nun, took a cutting of it over the water to the island of Sri Lanka. King Devanampiya Tissa set it in the ground at Anuradhapura, his capital, where it still grows as the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, the oldest tree in the world planted by people on a recorded date. It is more than 2,300 years old.

Back in India, the Bodh Gaya tree died and regrew several times, and in 1876 a storm killed the last old one. Five years later, in 1881, Alexander Cunningham, a British archaeologist, replanted the site with a cutting from its own descendant in Sri Lanka, so the tree's child returned home to replace its parent.

borobudur.context_blurb:
In the green heart of Java, ringed by smoking volcanoes, stands Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth. Builders piled grey volcanic stone into a stepped mountain in the 9th century, then the world forgot it for hundreds of years. Pilgrims do not go inside it; they climb it, and the climb is the whole point.

Seen from above, Borobudur is a mandala, a sacred map of the universe used in Buddhist and Hindu meditation, built in stone so that people can walk it. Its square base runs about 123 metres a side and rises through six square platforms and three round ones to a central dome.

The monument has no rooms at all, so a pilgrim walks every gallery from the bottom to the top, always turning clockwise with the monument on the right, a spiralling journey of more than 5 kilometres. The long walk itself is the pilgrimage, a slow rise from everyday life toward enlightenment.

Ringing the circular upper terraces stand 72 stone bells pierced with small openings, and inside each one sits a stone Buddha, seated in meditation, half hidden in shadow. Counting the statues in niches below, Borobudur holds 504 Buddhas.

For centuries after it was abandoned, eruptions from nearby volcanoes dusted it layer by layer until it lay buried under volcanic ash, and jungle grew over the mound until it looked like an ordinary wooded hill. The volcano that still looms over it is Mount Merapi, one of the most active on Earth, which coated the temple in ash again in 2010. That same restless landscape made the fertile plain around it and the stone it is built from.

The climb passes through three planes of the Buddhist universe, from earthly craving at the base, up through square terraces crowded with carvings of gods and stories. The circular terraces at the summit are Arupadhatu, the formless world, where the carvings stop and only the stupas remain.

The holes in those stone bells change as the pilgrim climbs: diamond-shaped on the two lower round terraces, square on the highest, so the Buddha inside grows harder to see as the summit nears. The change is meant to show form itself fading away as enlightenment approaches.

The monument also hides a secret storey. Its true base was walled inside a thick stone platform, sealing away 160 carved panels. They show the law of karma, with good deeds bringing rewards and cruel deeds bringing punishment, and they were found by chance in 1885, photographed, and covered again, with only one corner left open.

The great central stupa at the very top held no finished Buddha like the others, only one rough, unfinished statue, now kept in the site museum. Some scholars think it was a mistake that was set aside; others think the roughness was deliberate, a picture of an enlightenment beyond shape. No one knows for sure.

By the 20th century, rainwater soaking the earth hill inside the monument made its terraces bulge and slide. So between 1975 and 1982 a rescue led by UNESCO took Borobudur completely apart, numbering more than a million stones, cleaning them and setting every one back on a new foundation with drains to keep the water out.

brasilia.context_blurb:
In the middle of Brazil, on a high, dry plateau far from the crowded Atlantic coast, a whole capital city was conjured out of empty scrubland in the late 1950s. President Juscelino Kubitschek wanted to pull his country inland, and the planner Lúcio Costa and the architect Oscar Niemeyer gave him Brasília, a city of sweeping concrete curves.

Brasília rose from bare ground in just 41 months, under 4 years, and took over from Rio de Janeiro as Brazil's capital on 21 April 1960.

The land around it is the cerrado, Brazil's great tropical savanna of grass and twisted trees, and the city stands about 1,170 metres up on a plateau, chosen as neutral ground far from the old coastal cities.

From the air Costa's master plan looks like a giant airplane, with two gently curved wings holding the homes and a long straight body holding the government buildings. Some say it looks more like a bird or a dragonfly. Costa himself said the design began with the most ancient gesture of someone claiming a place, two lines crossing at right angles, the very sign of the Cross. The east-west axis holds the ministries; the curved north-south axis holds the housing.

Niemeyer's cathedral is a ring of 16 bent white columns of concrete that lean together and hold up a roof of glass, and Brazilians call it a crown of thorns. Niemeyer said the columns were like two hands reaching up to heaven.

A capital needs water, even on a dry plateau. Engineers built a dam across the Paranoá River and let the valley flood, creating Lake Paranoá, which curls around the city lined with sailboats and lakeside palaces. The dam opened on 12 September 1959, Kubitschek's birthday.

The city's most photographed building is the National Congress: two slim twin towers between two great white bowls, one opening upward for the Chamber of Deputies, open to the people, and one turned over as a dome for the Senate, a symbol of careful thought. In 1987 Brasília became a World Heritage Site for its modern design.
