dallol-and-the-danakil-depression.context_blurb:
In the Afar region of northern Ethiopia, the land sinks into the Danakil Depression, one of the lowest, hottest and strangest places on Earth. Here the crust is slowly tearing apart. Pools of acid steam among crusts of salt in impossible colours, lava churns in an open crater, and Afar miners still cut salt by hand as their ancestors did.

At Dallol, steaming pools of neon green, yellow and orange sit on twisted salt, a landscape so alien that scientists study it as a stand-in for Mars. The Danakil around it is the hottest place on Earth by year-round average, near 35 °C, and its floor lies about 120 metres below sea level.

The colours are painted by minerals, not living things: as scalding brine wells up and dries, dissolved iron and sulphur, along with copper, crystallise out in bands of green, gold and orange. Magma only a few kilometres down heats the water so fiercely, and fills it with so much sulphur, that some pools reach a pH below zero, about as acidic as battery acid.

Beneath the depression the salt runs as deep as two kilometres, laid down as an arm of the Red Sea flooded the sinking basin again and again and then dried away in the desert sun. For centuries Afar miners have cut that salt into flat slabs called amole, loaded about forty onto each camel, and carried them to the highlands, where the slabs served Ethiopians as money.

The Danakil sits on the Afar Triple Junction, where the African, Arabian and Somali plates are pulling apart a centimetre or two each year, and geologists expect that in millions of years the sea will pour in and the basin will become a whole new ocean.

A short trek away stands Erta Ale, the smoking mountain in the Afar language. Its lava lake has stayed molten since 1906 or earlier, longer than any other, and such open lakes of lava are so uncommon that in 2019 there were only about eight on the entire planet.

damascus.context_blurb:
Damascus, the capital of Syria, grew up in an oasis where mountain water meets the desert at the eastern edge of the Mediterranean world. It has been a city for thousands of years, and in the 7th century it became the capital of the Umayyad caliphs, rulers of the first great Islamic empire. Its old streets still follow a Roman plan.

Jericho was founded earlier, but its people abandoned it again and again, while Damascus was a thriving settlement by 2000 BC and has never been emptied since, so it has a strong claim to be the oldest continuously inhabited city in the world. Aleppo and Byblos are its chief rivals for that title.

The Barada River, fed by mountain snowmelt in the Anti-Lebanon range, fans out across the plain into the Ghouta, the ring of watered orchards and fields that has kept the city alive since ancient times. Damascus sits about 680 metres up and some 80 kilometres from the sea.

At the heart of the old city stands the Umayyad Mosque, begun in 706 by the caliph al-Walid I on ground already holy for millennia, where Hadad the storm god, then the Roman Jupiter and then Christian worshippers had each had their temple or church. About 12,000 labourers built it, and gold mosaics of a green, watery paradise covered some 4,000 square metres of its walls. Inside, a small domed shrine is said to hold John the Baptist's head, and Christians and Muslims, who honour him as the prophet Yahya, pray there side by side. Several other places also claim the relic; the shrine rests on tradition, not proof.

The old Roman main avenue, about 1,500 metres long, is the Street Called Straight, where in the Book of Acts a disciple named Ananias is sent to find Saul of Tarsus, newly blinded, who would become the apostle Paul.

The city also gave its name to a legendary steel. Blades rippled with watery patterns were forged and traded here, though the raw steel came from India and Sri Lanka. By about 1900 the craft had stopped, and the exact method was lost and has never been fully recovered. Scholars still argue about just how the old smiths did it.

damascus-steel-the-lost-watered-blades.context_blurb:
Between about the 9th and 17th centuries, smiths in the Islamic world forged sword blades famous for their beauty and their edge. Across the polished steel ran dark, rippling bands like flowing water. The blades carried the name of the Syrian city where many were sold, but their secret came from far away, and in time it was forgotten.

The rippling pattern was part of the metal, forged into the blade from within, made by microscopic bands of hard carbide crystals locked into the steel. It was not paint added afterwards. The Arabic word damas behind the name also means watered, a perfect fit for those ripples, which is why the metal is still called watered or damask steel.

Syria made no such steel itself: it imported little cakes of steel called wootz, made far to the east in India and Sri Lanka, and Damascus smiths forged them into swords. In Sri Lanka, smiths sealed iron with carbon-rich bamboo and leaves in clay pots and let the monsoon winds blow their furnaces hot enough to melt it into steel unusually rich in carbon. The word wootz comes from a Tamil word meaning to melt.

The blades cut so well that legends grew around them. The most famous tale claims a true Damascus blade could slice a wisp of silk that simply drifted down onto its edge, though no one ever proved it.

As the supply of wootz dried up, the craft faded, and by about 1900 the knowledge of how to make true Damascus steel had died out and been forgotten. The last eyewitness account of the old process was recorded in 1903. In the 1990s the metallurgists John Verhoeven and Alfred Pendray recreated the pattern and found that a trace of vanadium in the Indian ore had been a hidden key.

In 2006 Peter Paufler's team in Dresden examined a 17th-century sabre under a powerful microscope and reported carbon nanotubes inside the steel, a claim other scientists still dispute. Long before, the great scientist Michael Faraday had tried to crack the secret and guessed wrong.

death-valley.context_blurb:
In eastern California, between steep mountain walls, lies Death Valley, the lowest, driest and hottest place in North America. Its floor sinks below sea level and its summer air can top 50 °C. The pioneers who named it expected to die there, yet the valley hides snow, wandering stones and sudden carpets of flowers.

In 1849 a party of Gold Rush families took a shortcut and were stranded for weeks until William Manly and John Rogers, both still young, walked out and returned with food, and despite the grim name one of them gave the valley as they left, just one of the party had died.

On 10 July 1913 the thermometer at Furnace Creek read 134 °F, or 56.7 °C, and the world's weather authority, the WMO, still lists it as the hottest air temperature ever measured on Earth. Some experts think the reading ran a little high, and the hottest readings of sun-baked ground are a separate record held elsewhere.

Badwater Basin, 282 feet below sea level, is the continent's lowest point on dry ground, yet just 15 miles away rises Telescope Peak, an 11,049-foot summit often capped with snow. Its floor is nearly 200 square miles of white salt that cracks into repeating hexagons as briny groundwater rises, evaporates and shrinks the crust. The salt is all that is left of an Ice Age lake.

Storms do blow in from the Pacific, but four mountain ranges stand in the way, and each one forces the clouds up and wrings out their rain and snow, so the air that reaches the valley is dry. That makes Death Valley a rain-shadow desert, with under two inches of rain a year.

No river carved the valley: the crust of the whole region is being stretched apart, and the valley floor keeps sinking a few millimetres deeper each year as fresh faults crack the ground.

On Racetrack Playa, rocks weighing up to 600 pounds sit at the ends of long trails across the dry lakebed, as if they had walked. In 2014 scientists filmed the answer: on rare winter nights a shallow pond freezes into thin sheets of ice, and a light breeze pushes the floating panels, which shove the rocks across the mud.

After an unusually wet winter, the bare floor bursts into sheets of yellow Desert Gold, because the flowers wait out the dry years as seeds lying dormant in the soil. Big superblooms came in 1998, 2005 and 2016.

delhi-the-city-of-seven-cities.context_blurb:
Delhi, on the Yamuna plain of northern India, is called the city of seven cities, because ruler after ruler built a new capital beside the old ones instead of reusing them. Hindu kings, sultans, Mughal emperors and the British all left monuments here, and more than a thousand years of history stand side by side among its traffic and gardens.

Its most famous tower is the Qutb Minar, begun in 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak, which rises 72.5 metres in bands of red and grey sandstone, ringed with balconies, the tallest brick minaret on Earth. In 1369 lightning shattered its top, and Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq repaired the crown, turning its old fourth storey into two, which gave the tower its five storeys.

Beside it stands the Quwwat-ul-Islam, Delhi's first mosque, begun in 1193, and an inscription over its gate states that its stone came from 27 Hindu and Jain temples pulled down to build it. The reused columns still show their old carvings of lotus flowers, bells and chains.

In the same courtyard stands a dark iron pillar about 7 metres tall and over 6 tonnes in weight, made in the Gupta era some 1,600 years ago. Ordinary iron standing outdoors that long would have rusted away, but this pillar has barely rusted at all. The metallurgist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur found the secret: the iron is unusually rich in phosphorus, which over time grows a thin protective film that heals itself, so an impurity, not purity, protects it. For centuries visitors believed a wish would come true if they stood with their backs to the pillar and stretched their arms around it until their fingertips met. So many hands rubbed it that a fence now guards it.

In the 1600s the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan made Delhi his capital and built the Red Fort beside the Yamuna, a palace-fortress of red sandstone whose walls run about 2.4 kilometres around halls and gardens. In its Hall of Private Audience, golden letters proclaim that if paradise exists anywhere in the world, this very hall is that paradise, and the verse says it is this three times over. There stood the Peacock Throne, a throne of solid gold, seven years in the making, that blazed with some 26,733 gems, including the Koh-i-Noor diamond. It was later carried off and broken up.

Humayun's Tomb, built between 1565 and 1572 as the first great garden-tomb in India, holds over a hundred members of the Mughal royal family and court, which earned it the nickname Dormitory of the Mughals. It stands in a charbagh, Persian for four gardens: a walled garden divided into four quarters by walkways and water channels that stand for the four rivers of paradise. Modelled on Timur's tomb in Samarkand, its white double dome rising over red sandstone led on to the greatest tomb of all, the Taj Mahal at Agra.

delphi-the-oracle-at-the-navel-of-the-wo.context_blurb:
High on a mountainside in central Greece, ringed by tall cliffs, lie the ruins of Delphi. For about a thousand years, kings, generals and ordinary Greeks climbed here to ask the god Apollo about the future, and the answers they received could launch wars and found cities. The Greeks believed this was the very centre of the world.

They called the spot the omphalos, the navel, so Delphi was the world's navel, marked by a carved stone shaped like a dome. Myth said Zeus released two eagles from the far ends of the earth, each speeding toward the other, and where they met, above Delphi, he set down the stone. The stone in the museum today is a Roman copy.

The temples and treasuries climb in terraces up the southern slopes of Mount Parnassus, high above the Gulf of Corinth.

Before it was Delphi the place was called Pytho, because legend said Apollo had killed a great serpent there, Python, that guarded the spring. From that serpent came the title of the priestess who spoke for Apollo: the Pythia, one of the most powerful women of the ancient world. Questions could be put to her on only one day each month.

Her answers were famous for their double meanings. When King Croesus asked whether to attack Persia and heard that a great empire would fall, he marched, lost, and the empire destroyed was his own kingdom of Lydia, conquered by Cyrus the Great. The historian Herodotus told the story.

The ancients said the Pythia sat on a three-legged seat over a cleft in the floor of the temple, breathing fumes that clouded her mind. In the 1980s and 1990s the geologist Jelle de Boer and the archaeologist John Hale found two faults crossing beneath the temple and proposed that earth movements released ethylene, a sweet-smelling gas once used to put patients to sleep. A spring near Delphi has shown traces of it, but the theory is still debated.

Over the doorway of Apollo's temple were carved short sayings of wisdom, the most famous being Know thyself, and beside it Nothing in excess. Every visitor read them on the way in.

denali.context_blurb:
In the heart of Alaska, the snowy bulk of Denali towers more than 20,000 feet over the forests and tundra, the highest peak in North America. It climbs almost straight from low ground instead of from a high plateau, and it stands so far north that its summit is one of the coldest places on the planet. For a century maps called it Mount McKinley; in 2015 it officially regained its old name.

The name comes from the Koyukon people, who have lived in the valleys around the mountain for countless generations, and in their language Denali means the High One.

In 2015 the US Geological Survey measured the peak with modern GPS and set its official height at 20,310 feet, ten feet less than the 1952 figure, not because the mountain shrank but because the measurement got sharper.

Of the Seven Summits, the highest peaks on each continent, Denali is the most northerly, at about 63 degrees north, just below the Arctic Circle. In December 2003 a station high on the mountain recorded a wind chill of about minus 118 °F, the lowest ever recorded in North America.

Denali's air is even thinner than its height suggests, because the atmosphere is squashed thinner over the polar regions than at the equator, so its summit feels like a far higher peak in the tropics. Climbers there struggle for breath as if they stood hundreds of metres higher.

From the lowland at its foot to its summit, Denali rises about 18,000 feet, more than Everest's own climb from base to top, because Everest starts from an already high plateau. Everest reaches higher above the sea, but it rises only about 12,000 to 15,000 feet above its own base.

Denali is still growing: along the great Denali Fault, the Pacific plate is grinding beneath the North American plate, pushing the whole Alaska Range upward. In another two million years the squeeze may lift it about a kilometre more.

devils-tower.context_blurb:
On the prairie of northeastern Wyoming, a colossal stump of grey rock stands about 265 metres high, its sides fluted with giant columns. Several Plains peoples hold it sacred and call it Bear Lodge. Geologists have puzzled over how it formed, and filmmakers made it one of the most recognisable shapes on Earth.

In Steven Spielberg's 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind, a man haunted by the tower's shape builds its shape at supper out of his mashed potatoes, and the aliens' mothership lands there at the end.

On 24 September 1906, using a brand-new law that let presidents protect natural wonders, Theodore Roosevelt made Devils Tower the first national monument in the United States.

Its columns formed the same way as those of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland: as a thick mass of molten rock cools, it shrinks and cracks apart into long four- to seven-sided columns. Here they reach up to about 600 feet tall.

The rock hardened underground about 40 million years ago inside softer layers of sediment, and over millions of years erosion stripped that soft rock away, leaving the hard core standing in the open. The tower was uncovered, not built up. It looks like an old volcano, but no eruption ever happened here: the surrounding rocks contain no volcanic ash at all, which an eruption would have left. Geologists still argue over exactly what kind of underground intrusion it was.

In a Kiowa story, seven girls fleeing a giant bear climbed onto a low rock that rose higher and higher, while the bear's claws raked the grooves down its sides, and the girls were carried up into the sky to become the Pleiades, the star cluster called the Seven Sisters. The name Devils Tower came from an 1875 expedition whose interpreter reportedly mistranslated the Lakota name, and many tribes ask that Bear Lodge be restored.

teaches.2bcb6139da: In Steven Spielberg's 1977 film Close Encounters of the Third Kind, a man haunted by the tower's shape builds its shape at supper out of his mashed potatoes, and the aliens' mothership lands there at the end.
teaches.21d603718a: On 24 September 1906, using a brand-new law that let presidents protect natural wonders, Theodore Roosevelt made Devils Tower the first national monument in the United States.
teaches.48f24bdab2: Its columns formed the same way as those of the Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland: as a thick mass of molten rock cools, it shrinks and cracks apart into long four- to seven-sided columns.
teaches.59905dd2a4: The rock hardened underground about 40 million years ago inside softer layers of sediment, and over millions of years erosion stripped that soft rock away, leaving the hard core standing in the open.
teaches.1704b75b19: It looks like an old volcano, but no eruption ever happened here: the surrounding rocks contain no volcanic ash at all, which an eruption would have left.

drainage-basins-and-the-continental-divi.context_blurb:
Every raindrop that lands on a continent is headed somewhere. Ridges and mountains sort the water into great natural regions, each draining to a single river mouth or lake, and the highest ridges decide which ocean the water will reach. In the Americas, one long ridge splits whole continents between the Pacific and the Atlantic.

The whole area of land that sends its water to a single river system is called a drainage basin, or watershed, and America's Mississippi collects the runoff of 31 states, nearly half the nation, and delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Continental Divide runs along the crest of the Rockies and on down the Andes, and rain falling on its western side flows to the Pacific Ocean, while water on the eastern side ends up in the Atlantic, much of it through the Gulf of Mexico. Where it crosses Colorado, the Divide reaches its North American summit on Grays Peak, 14,278 feet high.

At Triple Divide Peak in Montana, meltwater from one summit runs to three seas: one creek to the Pacific, one to the Gulf of Mexico, and a third north across Canada by the Nelson River into Hudson Bay.

At Two Ocean Pass in Wyoming's Teton Wilderness, a creek climbs right onto the Divide and splits in two: one half flows as Atlantic Creek some 3,488 miles to the Gulf of Mexico, the other as Pacific Creek 1,353 miles to the Pacific. It is said a fish could swim across the Continental Divide here.

In southern Wyoming the Divide splits and loops around the Great Divide Basin, an endorheic basin, sealed off from every ocean, where rain and snow simply pool and evaporate.

The biggest drainage basin on Earth belongs to the Amazon, about 7 million square kilometres, roughly 40 percent of South America, spread across nine countries. In Africa, the mighty Congo River loops twice across the equator on a journey of some 4,700 kilometres, draining a vast rainforest, and empties into the Atlantic Ocean at the Gulf of Guinea.

In southern Venezuela the Casiquiare channel breaks away from the upper Orinoco and carries part of its water about 320 kilometres into the Rio Negro, joining the Orinoco to the Amazon, the largest natural link between two great river basins. Alexander von Humboldt confirmed it in 1800.

In 2016 Canada's retreating Kaskawulsh Glacier switched its meltwater away from the Slims River, which flows north, and into a neighbouring river that runs to the Gulf of Alaska, the first river capture scientists ever watched as it happened. Within a single year the Slims ran nearly dry. Geologists think the Casiquiare may slowly be capturing the upper Orinoco in the same way.

drumlins-and-eskers-streamlined-hills-an.context_blurb:
During the last ice age, great ice sheets crept across much of northern Europe and North America. When they melted, they left behind shapes that still mark the land: smooth whaleback hills and long winding ridges of gravel. Read them correctly and they become a map of where the vanished ice once flowed.

Boston's Breed's Hill, where the Battle of Bunker Hill was fought in 1775, is a drumlin, a smooth, egg-shaped hill that a passing ice sheet moulded from the rubble it dragged beneath itself. The word comes from an Irish word for a little ridge, and Boston sits on more than a hundred of them.

In Clew Bay on Ireland's west coast, the sea flooded a field of drumlins after the ice age, leaving a scatter of round green islands, and a local saying claims there is one island for every day of the year.

A drumlin works like a frozen compass: its blunt, steep end faces back toward where the ice came from, and its long gentle tail points the way the ice flowed, so a whole field of them records the direction of the vanished glacier. Between Rochester and Syracuse in New York lie roughly 10,000 drumlins, shaped by the great ice sheet about 18,000 years ago.

An esker is a long, winding ridge of sorted sand and gravel laid down by a river that flowed in a tunnel beneath the glacier, so that when the ice was gone, the old riverbed remained as a raised bank. In Sweden, the Uppsala esker runs about 250 kilometres, straight through the city of Uppsala.

Because eskers stand raised and dry above bog, they made natural roads. In Ireland the chain called the Eiscir Riada carried the Great Way between Dublin and Galway. Old Irish legend says that when Conn and Mug Nuadat fought at Magh Léna some eighteen centuries ago, the ridge served as the line that split Ireland in two between rival kings, Conn of the Hundred Battles in the north and Mug Nuadat in the south.

In eastern Finland the Punkaharju esker winds 7 kilometres along a narrow neck of land between the lakes Puruvesi and Pihlajavesi, so slender in places that a road and a railway squeeze along its crest side by side. Tsar Alexander I admired it on a visit in 1802 and asked that it be preserved, and in 1843 Finland protected it, making it one of the earliest protected natural areas in the world.

dubai.context_blurb: Dubai is a city-state on the Persian Gulf coast of the United Arab Emirates. Within living memory it was a small desert port whose economy ran on pearling and the dhow trade with India and East Africa. From the 1970s on, oil money and then explicit government policy transformed it into one of the most relentlessly built-up cities on Earth, with the world's tallest skyscraper rising from the desert, artificial palm-shaped islands reclaimed from the sea, and indoor ski slopes beside the mall.

dubrovnik.context_blurb: Dubrovnik is a small Croatian city on the Adriatic coast, protected by a complete, walkable ring of medieval stone city walls. For centuries it existed as a tiny maritime trading republic — the Republic of Ragusa — that cleverly outmaneuvered the Venetians, the Ottomans, and the Habsburgs to stay independent. Its merchants rivalled Venice's. The old city, famously filmed as 'King's Landing' in the Game of Thrones TV series, is a tight warren of smooth-paved marble streets and terracotta roofs inside the walls.

easter-island-rapa-nui.context_blurb: Easter Island — called Rapa Nui by its own people — is one of the most isolated inhabited islands on Earth, in the far southeastern Pacific. Polynesian settlers arrived there sometime between about 900 and 1200 CE. Over the following centuries they carved and raised nearly a thousand enormous stone statues of ancestral figures, called moai. The population later collapsed, through some combination of ecological strain, European contact, slave raids, and introduced diseases. The island is a Chilean possession today, and its people are still here.

egyptian-hieroglyphs-and-the-rosetta-sto.context_blurb: Egyptian hieroglyphs are the picture-based writing system used for sacred and monumental texts throughout the three thousand years of pharaonic civilization. After the Roman era, no one could read them anymore, and for about 1,400 years the elaborate carvings in Egyptian temples were a complete mystery. The key to cracking them turned out to be a slab of stone that soldiers in Napoleon's 1799 Egyptian campaign stumbled on near a village in the Nile Delta: it bore the same royal decree carved in three scripts, one of which was readable Greek. A French scholar, Jean-Francois Champollion, eventually used it to unlock the hieroglyphs in the 1820s.

el-nino-and-la-nina-the-pacific-that-shi.context_blurb: El Nino and La Nina are the two phases of a natural climate cycle in the tropical Pacific Ocean. Normally the trade winds push warm surface water westward, piling it up near Indonesia and letting cold deep water rise near South America. In an El Nino year that pattern breaks down and the warm water sloshes east; in a La Nina year it is reinforced. The resulting shifts in sea temperatures ripple through the atmosphere and change weather patterns across much of the world — floods in some places, droughts in others, fewer or more hurricanes.

ellora-kailasa-temple.context_blurb: At the Ellora caves in western India stands what may be the most audacious single sculpture ever made. The Kailasa Temple, honouring the Hindu god Shiva, is not a built temple at all; it was carved downward out of a single cliff of solid basalt in the 8th century CE, with full courtyards, towers, elephants, and pillars all left standing as the surrounding rock was cut away. The volume of stone removed to free it is staggering.

endorheic-basins-water-with-no-way-out-t.context_blurb: An endorheic basin is a drainage basin from which no water ever reaches the ocean. Rain and snowmelt flow in but can only escape by evaporation. Over long time scales this concentrates whatever salts and minerals the inflow carried, so endorheic basins often hold salty lakes, salt flats, or expanses of mineral-crusted desert. The Caspian Sea, Great Salt Lake, Lake Chad, the Aral Sea, and the Bolivian Salar de Uyuni are all endorheic. About 18 percent of the Earth's land surface drains to no sea at all.

estuaries-and-tidal-bores-where-river-me.context_blurb: An estuary is the stretch of a river where fresh water meets and mixes with the salt water of the sea, usually at the river's mouth. Estuaries are among the most biologically productive habitats on Earth, nurseries for fish and shellfish. Many of them show interesting hydrology: as the tide pushes salty water upstream, the fresh river water sits above it in a wedge-shaped layer. In narrow, funnel-shaped estuaries, the rising tide can even combine into a travelling wave that races upriver, called a tidal bore.

etna-stromboli-and-the-word-volcano.context_blurb: Along the coast of Italy and Sicily sit several of the most famous active volcanoes on Earth. Mount Etna on Sicily is Europe's tallest active volcano and one of the most active anywhere; it has been erupting on and off for thousands of years. Just offshore to the north, the small volcanic island of Stromboli has been in a state of near-continuous mild eruption for several thousand years. The English word 'volcano' itself comes from another island of this chain, Vulcano, which the Romans believed to be the forge of their god of fire.

fado-lisbon.context_blurb: Fado is the melancholic urban folk music of Portugal, born in the port-side neighborhoods of Lisbon in the first half of the 19th century. Its name comes from the Latin fatum ('fate'). It is typically sung by a solo singer accompanied by a classical guitar and a distinctively pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, and its lyrics are preoccupied with a particular Portuguese emotion of bittersweet longing for things lost or far away. In 2011 UNESCO added fado to its list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

fatehpur-sikri-the-abandoned-red-city.context_blurb: Fatehpur Sikri, in northern India near Agra, is a perfectly preserved red-sandstone imperial city built in the late 16th century by the Mughal emperor Akbar as his new capital. Akbar held religious debates in it between Muslims, Hindus, Christians, Jains, and Zoroastrians, trying to arrive at a sort of universal faith. Then, after only a handful of years, the city was abandoned, apparently because its water supply failed. It stands today in near-mint condition as a frozen snapshot of the Mughal court at its most ambitious.

fes.context_blurb: Fes (Fez), in Morocco, was founded in the 8th century CE and became for a time the capital of a succession of medieval Muslim dynasties in North Africa. Its old walled medina — a maze of lanes too narrow for cars — is one of the largest living medieval urban environments anywhere, little changed in a thousand years. Donkeys still carry loads through its alleys. Fes is home to what is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world, founded in 859 by a Tunisian woman named Fatima al-Fihri.

fjords-drowned-glacier-valleys.context_blurb: A fjord is a deep, narrow sea-inlet with high, often sheer, rock walls. Fjords form where glaciers running down to the sea gouged out deep U-shaped valleys during an ice age; when the ice melted and sea levels rose, the sea flooded in and drowned the valleys. Norway's long western coast is famous for its fjords; others carve the coasts of Chile, New Zealand, Alaska, Greenland, and the Canadian Arctic. The water in them can be deeper than the open ocean just outside the fjord's mouth.

flamenco-andalusia.context_blurb: Flamenco is the dance and music tradition born in Andalusia, the southernmost region of Spain, out of a centuries-long cultural mix: Andalusian, Roma, Jewish, and Moorish. It combines passionate guitar playing, hand-clapping, foot-stamping, singing, and dance in a highly structured but intensely emotional performance. Different flamenco 'palos' (styles) carry very different moods, from grief-stricken siguiriya to joyful alegrias. UNESCO recognized flamenco in 2010 as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

florence-brunelleschis-impossible-dome.context_blurb: Florence, in Tuscany, Italy, was the city where the Renaissance began. Under the enormous wealth and patronage of the Medici family of bankers, it produced a staggering roster of 15th- and 16th-century painters, sculptors, and architects — Donatello, Botticelli, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci. Its cathedral is crowned by a vast red-brick dome designed by the goldsmith-turned-architect Filippo Brunelleschi, who had to invent entirely new techniques to build the biggest dome anyone had attempted since Roman times.

foehn-and-chinook-the-warm-wind-off-the-.context_blurb: When moist air is forced up and over a mountain range, it drops its rain on the windward side; by the time it reaches the leeward slope it is dry. As it then sinks down the far side, the air is compressed and warms rapidly, sometimes dramatically — temperatures can rise by 20 degrees Celsius in minutes. In the Alps this warm dry downslope wind is called the Foehn; in the Rockies the Chinook; in southern California the Santa Ana; in Argentina the Zonda. The phenomenon has been linked to headaches, forest fires, and avalanches.

from-rift-to-ocean-the-red-sea-and-the-a.context_blurb: Where two continental tectonic plates pull apart, a long linear valley slowly opens between them, called a rift. If the rift keeps spreading long enough, the sea eventually floods in and a new ocean basin is born. The Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden are examples of rifts that have reached the ocean stage; the East African Rift to their south is a continental rift that is still in its earlier stages. At the Afar Triangle in Ethiopia, three plates meet and are tearing one of the strangest low-lying hot landscapes on the planet.

g-bekli-tepe.context_blurb: On a hilltop in southeastern Turkey stands a cluster of carved stone pillars arranged in rings, decorated with reliefs of foxes, snakes, scorpions, and birds. What makes them extraordinary is their age: about 11,500 years old, which means they were raised by Stone Age people before the invention of pottery, metal, or farming. Gobekli Tepe has rewritten the textbook timeline of civilization, suggesting that organized ritual and monumental building came before agriculture, not after. Equally strange, the whole site was deliberately buried under rubble around 8000 BCE and forgotten for ten thousand years.

ggantija-and-maltas-megalithic-temples.context_blurb: The tiny Mediterranean island nation of Malta hides a staggering secret: its stone temples are older than the Egyptian pyramids. Built by a mysterious prehistoric people roughly 5,500 years ago, the Ggantija temples on Gozo are among the oldest free-standing structures ever raised anywhere. Local legend said they were built by a race of giants, which is where the name comes from. The civilisation that built them later vanished without obvious explanation.

giant-waves-and-where-the-sea-floor-buil.context_blurb: Some stretches of coastline consistently produce the biggest ocean waves on Earth. Nazare on the Portuguese coast is one; Teahupo'o in Tahiti is another; Mavericks on the California coast is a third. The reason is almost always the shape of the sea floor just offshore. Deep underwater canyons focus incoming swells and funnel their energy toward the surface, so that waves which look ordinary further out suddenly rear up into towering walls just before they hit the beach. These spots have become legendary in big-wave surfing.

giants-causeway-and-fingals-cave.context_blurb: Along the north coast of Northern Ireland, a stretch of the shore is paved with roughly 40,000 interlocking black stone columns, mostly hexagonal, stepping out into the sea. On the opposite side of the water, on the Scottish island of Staffa, Fingal's Cave is a natural cathedral formed from the same honeycomb columns. Both were formed about 60 million years ago when enormous sheets of lava cooled and cracked in orderly polygonal patterns. The local Irish legend attributes them to a battle between two giants, one Irish and one Scottish.

glacial-erratics-boulders-the-ice-carrie.context_blurb: A glacial erratic is a large boulder sitting at the surface of the land whose rock type does not match the bedrock around it, because an ice-age glacier picked it up somewhere far away and dropped it off when the ice melted. Some erratics are the size of houses. In 19th-century Europe, before glaciation was understood, erratics were often explained as having been left by the biblical Flood; the Swiss geologist Louis Agassiz was one of the first to argue they had been moved by ice.

gondar.context_blurb: Gondar, in the mountains of northern Ethiopia, was the imperial capital of the Christian kingdom of Ethiopia from the 17th into the 19th century. Its emperors built a cluster of stone castles there — real European-style castles with crenellated walls and towers — which looks surprising enough that visitors sometimes rub their eyes. Ethiopia was never colonized, so the royal line goes back in an unbroken thread to its ancient roots; the Gondar castles are evidence of a confident, outward-looking court that borrowed what it fancied from the wider world.

gor-e-island.context_blurb: Goree is a small island just off the coast of Dakar, in modern Senegal, that was fought over and traded between the Portuguese, Dutch, English, and French for several centuries. It is remembered today chiefly as a site of the Atlantic slave trade. Its 'House of Slaves,' with its narrow passages and a doorway opening onto the water, has become a place of pilgrimage, visited by both Nelson Mandela and Barack Obama; serious historians argue over how many Africans actually passed through this specific island, but it remains a powerful symbol of a brutal chapter in history.

granada-the-alhambras-water-palace.context_blurb: Granada, in southern Spain, was the last Muslim-ruled kingdom in Western Europe. For centuries after the rest of the Iberian Peninsula had been reconquered by Christian kings, Granada held out as the capital of the small Nasrid emirate; it finally fell in 1492 to Ferdinand and Isabella. On a hill above the city stands the Alhambra palace-fortress, a masterpiece of Islamic architecture: a complex of courtyards, fountains, and halls whose walls are covered in intricate stucco calligraphy and geometric patterns.

great-zimbabwe.context_blurb: Great Zimbabwe is the ruin of a medieval African city in the south of today's country of Zimbabwe, which is actually named after it. From roughly the 11th to the 15th centuries it was the thriving capital of a wealthy Shona kingdom that controlled the inland trade in gold and ivory, selling it on toward the Indian Ocean coast. Its most famous surviving feature is the Great Enclosure, a towering circuit of stone walls built entirely without mortar, with a mysterious conical tower rising inside. For centuries European visitors refused to believe Africans could have built it; modern archaeology has settled that argument.

groundwater-the-hidden-rivers-under-our-.context_blurb: Groundwater is water held underground in the tiny spaces inside porous rock and soil, in layers called aquifers. It is replenished by rainwater soaking down from the surface over long periods — sometimes thousands of years. Across much of the world, from the US Great Plains to north Africa to north China, agriculture and cities depend heavily on pumping groundwater. In some places this pumping is now extracting water much faster than nature puts it back, with consequences from sinking land to drying wells.

gyeongju-the-museum-without-walls.context_blurb: Gyeongju, in southeastern South Korea, was for a thousand years the capital of the Silla kingdom, which eventually unified the Korean peninsula around the 7th century. The whole city is studded with grassy royal burial mounds that look like small natural hills but are actually gigantic tombs full of golden crowns, jewelry, and horse-fittings. Pagodas, Buddhist carvings, and old temples are everywhere. Gyeongju is sometimes called 'the museum without walls' because so much of its ancient fabric is scattered across the modern town.

ha-long-bay.context_blurb: Ha Long Bay, on the northern coast of Vietnam, is a scatter of hundreds of steep-sided limestone pinnacles and islets rising out of the sea. The towers are what geologists call 'drowned tower karst': they were once hills in a limestone landscape on dry land, until the sea rose at the end of the last Ice Age and flooded the valleys between them. According to Vietnamese tradition, the islands were made when a dragon spat jewels into the sea.

hangul-the-alphabet-korea-designed-on-pu.context_blurb: Hangul is the alphabet used today for the Korean language. Unlike most writing systems, which evolved slowly over centuries, Hangul was deliberately designed from scratch by a single person: King Sejong the Great, who announced it in 1446. He explicitly wanted a system simple enough that any Korean farmer could learn to read and write, instead of relying on the thousands of Chinese characters that only an elite could master. Hangul's letters are famously systematic — each one is shaped to resemble the position of the mouth, tongue, and throat when making that sound.

hanoi-old-quarter.context_blurb: Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, grew up on the banks of the Red River in the north of the country. For the last thousand years it has been one of the great cities of Vietnam, which spent much of its history fending off China from the north and (in modern times) France and the United States from across the oceans. The 'Old Quarter' is a dense 36-street warren of narrow 'tube houses,' each lane traditionally dedicated to selling a single kind of good — silver, silk, bamboo, tin — a layout that still shapes the neighbourhood today.

harar.context_blurb: Harar is a walled Muslim city in eastern Ethiopia that for centuries guarded a crossroads of the trans-African caravan trade. Its old quarter is a tight medieval warren of lanes behind thick stone walls, with dozens of small mosques inside, and it is traditionally counted as one of the great holy cities of the Muslim world. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud lived here for years as a trader after giving up poetry. Harar is also famous for a peculiar nightly ritual that takes place just outside its walls after dark.

harris-tweed-the-cloth-protected-by-law.context_blurb: Harris Tweed is a kind of thick woollen cloth woven on the Outer Hebrides islands of northwestern Scotland. The weavers live and work in the Isle of Harris, Lewis, Uist, and Barra. Harris Tweed is so distinctive that in 1909 the British Parliament passed a law reserving its name for cloth woven at the weavers' own homes from pure virgin wool, dyed and spun in the Outer Hebrides, and stamped by the industry's own authentication board. It is the only textile in the world protected by an Act of Parliament.

havana.context_blurb: Havana is the capital of Cuba, founded by the Spanish in 1519 on an excellent natural harbour on the island's north coast. For centuries it was the fortified gathering-point of Spain's silver-fleet convoys back to Europe. In 1959 Fidel Castro's revolution took power, Cuba became a Soviet ally, and the United States imposed a long embargo. Havana's old quarter, suspended somewhere between gorgeously faded Spanish-colonial grandeur and 1950s Chevrolets, is now one of the most atmospheric city centres in the Americas.

hip-hop-the-bronx.context_blurb: Hip-hop was born in the 1970s in the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of New York City. In its early years it coalesced out of block parties, basement discotheques, and DJ battles in the then-poor Bronx neighborhoods. From that scene emerged four fundamental elements — DJing, MCing (rapping), breakdancing, and graffiti art — that together make up hip-hop culture. Within fifty years it had become probably the single most influential cultural movement of the late 20th and early 21st centuries, dominating global popular music.

hiroshima-the-city-that-came-back.context_blurb: Hiroshima is a Japanese city on the southwestern coast of Honshu. On August 6, 1945, the United States dropped the first atomic bomb ever used in war on it, killing tens of thousands outright and tens of thousands more from radiation sickness and injury. In the decades since, the city has rebuilt itself and become a global symbol of peace. At the hypocentre, a single ruined domed building has been left standing in its blasted state as a memorial, while the surrounding streets throng with ordinary modern life.

hoi-an.context_blurb: Hoi An is a small town on the central coast of Vietnam. Between about the 15th and 19th centuries it was one of the busiest trading ports in Southeast Asia, with Japanese, Chinese, Dutch, Portuguese, and French merchants all based there. When the river harbour silted up, trade moved elsewhere and Hoi An slept. Its old quarter — a mix of wooden Chinese shophouses, a Japanese covered bridge, and French-colonial additions — survived almost intact. Today it is beautifully lit at night by thousands of coloured silk lanterns strung across its lanes.

holy-confluences-and-the-lowest-river-on.context_blurb: Many religions treat the place where two rivers join — a confluence — as particularly sacred, because the mixing of waters is an obvious symbol of unity. The most famous example is the Sangam at Prayagraj in northern India, where the Ganges meets the Yamuna and a tradition says they are joined underneath by a third, invisible, mythical river. Every twelve years tens of millions of Hindu pilgrims gather there for the Kumbh Mela. Elsewhere in sacred geography, the Jordan River flows down to the lowest point on Earth.

hong-kong-the-vertical-city.context_blurb: Hong Kong is a cluster of islands and a bit of mainland in the Pearl River Delta of southern China. For 150 years it was a British colony, which is why its civic life is a strange blend of Chinese and English habits. Returned to Chinese sovereignty in 1997, it has one of the most dramatic urban landscapes on Earth: steep green hills tumbling straight into a sheltered harbour, with its downtown pinned between them in a wall of improbably slender skyscrapers. It has long been one of Asia's great financial centres and probably the city with the most skyscrapers in the world.

hotspots-the-island-chains-a-drifting-pl.context_blurb: A 'hotspot' is a plume of unusually hot material rising from deep inside the Earth that stays roughly fixed while the tectonic plate above it drifts past. The hotspot melts the overlying plate again and again, building a chain of volcanoes. The Hawaiian island chain is the textbook example: the active volcano is at one end of the chain, and the islands get older and more weathered the further you move along it, charting the direction the Pacific plate has been moving over tens of millions of years. Yellowstone is another, less obvious, example.

hue-imperial-citadel.context_blurb: Hue, on the Perfume River in central Vietnam, was the imperial capital of Vietnam under the Nguyen dynasty from 1802 to 1945. In its centre is a huge moated and walled imperial citadel, modelled consciously on Beijing's Forbidden City. Much of it was heavily damaged during the Battle of Hue in 1968, one of the longest and bloodiest engagements of the Vietnam War, and some of it has only recently been restored.

hurricane-typhoon-cyclone-one-storm-thre.context_blurb: A hurricane, a typhoon, and a cyclone are the same kind of storm — a rotating tropical system of thunderstorms organized around a low-pressure centre — called by different names in different parts of the world. 'Hurricane' is used in the Atlantic and the northeastern Pacific, 'typhoon' in the northwestern Pacific, and simply 'cyclone' in the South Pacific and Indian Oceans. All of them form over warm tropical seas and feed on the energy of warm sea-surface water. Their most dangerous feature is often not the wind itself but the storm surge they push ahead of them.

ice-age-megafloods-and-vanished-lakes.context_blurb: At the end of the last Ice Age, as the great North American ice sheet melted, water piled up behind glacier-ice dams in enormous lakes. From time to time those dams broke. The results were megafloods — catastrophic torrents that lasted days or weeks, released more water than the combined flow of all the modern rivers on Earth, and ripped huge channels across the landscape. One such flood system, in what is now eastern Washington state, carved out the strange, scoured Channeled Scablands.

icebergs-how-they-calve-and-drift.context_blurb: Icebergs are chunks of freshwater ice that have broken off ('calved') from the edges of glaciers or ice shelves and drifted out into the sea. Most of the mass of an iceberg sits underwater, with only a small part showing above the surface. In the Southern Hemisphere, Antarctic ice shelves calve giant tabular icebergs; the biggest ever recorded was larger than the island of Jamaica. In the Northern Hemisphere, icebergs mostly come from the glaciers of Greenland and drift south in the Labrador Current, which is where the Titanic struck one in 1912.

iceland-where-two-continents-pull-apart.context_blurb: Iceland sits in the middle of the North Atlantic, straddling the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates are pulling apart. The island is literally splitting in half, a few centimetres per year. New land is also forming all the time: Iceland is one of the most volcanically active places on Earth, with eruptions somewhere on the island on average every few years. The combination of hot volcanic rock close to the surface and abundant rain-and-snowmelt makes Iceland the world's leader in geothermal energy.

iguaz-falls.context_blurb: Iguazu Falls crashes down a long curved cliff on the border of Argentina and Brazil, in the subtropical rainforests of South America. Rather than one broad sheet, the river splits over the edge into a long chain of individual cascades divided by lush rocky islands, so visitors can walk among the different drops. Depending on the water level the number of cascades varies, but it is always far more than Niagara. When the American First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt first saw the falls, she is said to have murmured, 'Poor Niagara!'

isfahan.context_blurb: Isfahan, in central Iran, was the capital of the Safavid Persian Empire in the 16th and 17th centuries under Shah Abbas the Great. A medieval Persian saying held that 'Isfahan is half the world,' and the shah built himself a city to match: an enormous central square ringed by palaces, a grand mosque, and a dazzling royal mosque, all faced in blue tilework. The Safavid Isfahan has survived largely intact; it is one of the most beautiful cities in the Islamic world.

isostatic-rebound-the-land-still-rising.context_blurb: The weight of a thick ice sheet pushes down on the Earth's crust, slowly bowing it into the softer mantle beneath. When the ice melts away, the crust springs back up — not all at once, but over thousands of years. This process is called isostatic rebound. It is still happening today in regions that were under the ice during the last Ice Age — Scandinavia, Scotland, and much of Canada are all literally rising upward every year, and the land along the Baltic coast of Sweden and Finland keeps gaining new metres of beachfront each generation.

istanbul.context_blurb: Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus strait in modern Turkey, with half the city in Europe and the other half in Asia. For most of its history it was Constantinople, capital first of the Christian Byzantine Empire from 330 CE and then, after the Ottoman conquest of 1453, capital of the Muslim Ottoman Empire for another 470 years. The city is layered: the great Byzantine cathedral of Hagia Sophia stands beside grand Ottoman mosques, built in deliberate imitation. The old walls that defended it for a thousand years still ring the historic peninsula.

jaipur-the-pink-city-and-its-stone-sky-m.context_blurb: Jaipur, in the desert state of Rajasthan in northwestern India, was founded in 1727 by Maharaja Jai Singh II. He was a serious astronomer as well as a king, and he laid out his new city on a geometric plan straight from classical Hindu town-planning texts. The old city was later painted a uniform warm pinkish red to welcome a visiting royal, and the colour has stuck. Jai Singh also built a bizarre open-air observatory of gigantic masonry sundials and quadrants there, built big because he mistrusted the little brass European instruments of his day.

jazz-new-orleans.context_blurb: Jazz was born in New Orleans at the turn of the 20th century, out of the extraordinary cultural blend of that city: African, Caribbean, French, Spanish, and Anglo-American traditions all layered on top of each other. Marching band music, blues, ragtime, church spirituals, and Creole songs all fed into it, and the result was a brand-new improvisational music built on syncopated rhythms, blue notes, and solo improvisation. From New Orleans it travelled up the Mississippi to Chicago and then east to New York, and from there to the world.

jerusalems-old-city-quarter-by-quarter.context_blurb: The old walled city of Jerusalem is the single most densely sacred square kilometre in the world. It is holy to the three Abrahamic faiths: for Jews, as the city of David and the site of the destroyed First and Second Temples; for Christians, as the city where Jesus was crucified and (they believe) rose from the dead; for Muslims, as the city from which Muhammad is held to have ascended on his Night Journey. The old city is traditionally divided into four quarters — Muslim, Christian, Jewish, and Armenian — tightly packed inside a 16th-century Ottoman wall.

jingdezhen-chinas-porcelain-capital.context_blurb: Jingdezhen, in Jiangxi province in southeastern China, has been China's porcelain-making capital for more than a thousand years. Imperial porcelain for the Chinese court was fired here from the 14th century onward. The clay around the town, mixed in the right proportions and fired at the right temperature, produces the thin, white, translucent ceramic that the English language simply calls 'china' after the country where it was invented. For centuries Europeans tried and failed to work out how to make it.

k2.context_blurb: K2 straddles the border of Pakistan and China in the Karakoram range. At 8,611 metres it is the second-highest mountain on Earth, only about 240 metres shorter than Everest, but it is a far more technical and dangerous climb. Roughly one in four climbers who has reached its summit has died either coming down or trying. K2 gets its utilitarian name from an old 19th-century British survey list; the mountain is in such a remote region that it has no widely-used local name.

kabuki-and-noh-japan.context_blurb: Noh and Kabuki are the two great traditional Japanese theatrical forms. Noh is the older of the two, dating to the 14th century: a slow, austere, highly stylized form of masked theatre favoured by the samurai elite. Kabuki arose in the early 1600s, more boisterous, colourful, and crowd-pleasing, drawing audiences from the merchant classes of the big cities. Both are still performed today, with roles passed from one generation of actors to the next within specific family lineages.

kano.context_blurb: Kano, in northern Nigeria, is one of the oldest cities of West Africa and for a thousand years has been a major terminus of the trans-Saharan caravan trade in salt, cloth, and leather. It is the heart of the Hausa people's homeland, now a city of several million, encircled by surviving stretches of a vast medieval earthen wall. Its dyeing pits, where cloth is turned deep indigo blue, have been in continuous use for about five hundred years.

karnak-and-ancient-thebes-luxor.context_blurb: Karnak, on the east bank of the Nile at modern Luxor, is the biggest religious complex ever built in the ancient world. Successive pharaohs across more than a thousand years each added their own temples, obelisks, chapels, and pylons to the site, piling up a sacred city of stone around a shared great temple to the god Amun-Ra. Its hall of columns is so dense and gigantic that walking into it feels like entering a petrified forest.

kente-the-ashanti-cloth-of-ghana.context_blurb: Kente is the brilliantly coloured strip-woven cloth of the Ashanti and Ewe peoples of Ghana and Togo in West Africa. Each piece is built up from narrow strips of handwoven fabric, about four inches wide, hand-sewn together edge to edge. Every pattern and colour combination carries a specific name and meaning, and traditional kente was once reserved for royalty. In modern times it has become a global symbol of African identity, worn at graduations and ceremonies far beyond West Africa.

kettle-lakes-where-buried-ice-melted.context_blurb: A kettle lake forms when a chunk of ice from a retreating glacier gets buried in sediment and then slowly melts under the ground. The ground above collapses and the resulting hollow fills with water. The thousands of small round lakes dotting places like Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ontario, and parts of Scandinavia are mostly kettle lakes. From the air, a landscape pocked with them looks almost like it was dimpled with a thumb.

khiva-the-walled-desert-city.context_blurb: Khiva is a tiny, almost perfectly preserved medieval walled city in the middle of a Central Asian desert, in modern Uzbekistan. It was once a notorious Silk Road slave market and the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. Its old quarter — the Itchan Kala — is enclosed by thick mud-brick ramparts and crammed with blue-tiled madrasas, minarets, and mausoleums packed into a small walkable rectangle, which looks like a stage set when the sun lights it up at dawn.

kilimanjaro.context_blurb: Kilimanjaro, in northern Tanzania near the Kenyan border, is the highest mountain in Africa and the tallest free-standing mountain in the world — a huge volcanic cone rising out of the East African savannah. It is capped by glaciers even though it sits only three degrees south of the equator, though those ice fields have been shrinking fast over the last century. Unlike most of the world's great peaks, Kilimanjaro can be hiked rather than technically climbed, which is why thousands of trekkers summit it each year.

kilwa-kisiwani.context_blurb: Kilwa Kisiwani is a tiny island just off the coast of today's Tanzania that was once the richest trading city of the East African 'Swahili Coast.' Between about 1100 and 1500 its merchants were middlemen between the gold mines of inland Africa and the great trade routes of the Indian Ocean, dealing with ships from Arabia, Persia, India, and China. The 14th-century Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta called it one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Its stone palaces, mosques, and harbour buildings now stand in ruin, but they are among the oldest surviving stone buildings in sub-Saharan Africa.

kintsugi-japans-golden-mending.context_blurb: Kintsugi is the traditional Japanese art of repairing broken pottery by filling the cracks with a lacquer mixed with powdered gold, silver, or platinum. The resulting mended object is not disguised to look unbroken; instead the repair is highlighted, so the piece's history of breakage becomes a visible, often beautiful, part of the finished object. The practice is tied to a Japanese aesthetic philosophy — wabi-sabi — that finds beauty in imperfection, age, and incompleteness.

knossos-the-minoan-palace-and-the-labyri.context_blurb: On the Greek island of Crete stand the ruins of the Bronze Age palace of Knossos, centre of the Minoan civilisation that flourished around 2000 to 1400 BCE. Its sprawling, many-roomed plan may be the real-world origin of the Greek legend of the Minotaur hidden in a maze. The palace's wall-paintings show elegant women, fantastical animals, and a dangerous athletic ritual involving charging bulls. In the early 1900s the archaeologist Sir Arthur Evans dug it up and controversially rebuilt large parts of it with modern materials — his restorations are what tourists see today.

konark-sun-temple.context_blurb: On the eastern coast of India in the state of Odisha stands the 13th-century Konark temple, dedicated to the Hindu sun-god Surya. The whole structure was designed to look like a cosmic vehicle: an immense stone building shaped as a chariot, complete with carved wheels, prancing horses, and intricate reliefs on every surface. European sailors used it as a landmark. Most of its tallest tower collapsed centuries ago, but what remains is one of the great sculptural achievements of medieval India.

krakatoa-1883-the-loudest-sound-on-earth.context_blurb: In August 1883, the small volcanic island of Krakatoa, in the Sunda Strait between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, exploded in one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recorded history. The main blast was heard thousands of kilometres away. The eruption triggered towering tsunamis that killed tens of thousands of people on surrounding coasts. Enough ash and sulphur was thrown into the stratosphere that global temperatures dropped by about a degree over the following years and sunsets everywhere turned strange colours.

krakow.context_blurb: Krakow is one of the oldest cities in Poland and was its royal capital from the 11th century until the court moved to Warsaw in 1596. The old town, built around a huge central market square, survived World War II nearly intact — unlike Warsaw, which was almost totally destroyed. Krakow is also the city where John Paul II was archbishop before being elected pope, and it sits very close to the German concentration camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau, a mere hour's drive away.

kyoto-the-thousand-year-capital-of-templ.context_blurb: Kyoto was the imperial capital of Japan for more than a thousand years, from 794 CE until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869. During the Second World War the United States specifically spared the city from heavy bombing because of its cultural importance, which means its wooden temples, stone-and-gravel gardens, Shinto shrines, and traditional geisha quarters survive essentially intact. It is home to seventeen UNESCO World Heritage sites. The classical arts of Japan — tea ceremony, ikebana, Noh drama, kaiseki cuisine — all took their mature form here.

la-paz-and-el-alto.context_blurb: La Paz, in Bolivia, is the highest capital city on Earth — not quite the official constitutional capital, but the de facto seat of government. It sits in a deep canyon in the Andes at around 3,600 metres above sea level. On the plateau above the canyon's rim sprawls El Alto, a vast younger city of indigenous Aymara migrants that has become one of the largest cities of Bolivia in its own right. Modern cable cars now shuttle commuters between the two levels.

lagos.context_blurb: Lagos, on the southwestern coast of Nigeria, is the largest city in Africa, and its population is still exploding — some projections make it the biggest city on Earth before this century is over. It sprawls across a long coastal lagoon in a tangle of islands, bridges, markets, and makeshift waterside settlements. It is a cultural powerhouse: 'Afrobeats' pop and Nollywood films, now a global presence, were both born here.

lahore-the-mughal-city-of-mosque-and-gar.context_blurb: Lahore, in modern Pakistan, was for a long stretch the most important city of the Mughal Empire alongside Delhi and Agra. Many of its emperors preferred it. Within the old city stand some of the great monuments of Mughal architecture: a huge fort, formal pleasure gardens laid out in the Persian style, and one of the largest mosques of the Islamic world, all built in the red sandstone and white marble that are the signature of their era. Lahore is also a city of poets; many of the most-loved poems of modern Urdu were written here.

lake-baikal.context_blurb: Lake Baikal, in southern Siberia, is the oldest, deepest, and largest-by-volume freshwater lake on Earth. It holds roughly one-fifth of all the unfrozen fresh surface water on the planet — more than all of North America's Great Lakes combined. Its basin is a crack in the Earth's crust that has been slowly widening for about 25 million years, and it is still growing. Baikal is home to many species of fish, seal, and sponge that live nowhere else in the world.

lake-natron.context_blurb: Lake Natron, in the Great Rift Valley of northern Tanzania, is a shallow, extremely alkaline soda lake. Its water comes out of the surrounding volcanic rocks loaded with sodium carbonate, which makes the lake caustic to the touch — stronger than ammonia — and gives it a deep red colour from the salt-loving microbes that thrive in it. The lake is a world-famous breeding site for the lesser flamingo, which eats those same microbes. Dead animals that fall in are sometimes pickled by the alkaline water into eerie mummified postures.

lake-nyos.context_blurb: Lake Nyos, in the mountains of northwestern Cameroon, is a deep volcanic crater lake. In August 1986, carbon dioxide gas seeping up from magma below suddenly erupted out of its depths in a single catastrophic blast. The dense gas poured down the surrounding valleys and silently suffocated roughly 1,700 people and thousands of livestock in nearby villages overnight. In the decades since, engineers have installed vertical pipes to slowly degas the lake and prevent a repeat.

lake-superior-and-the-great-lakes.context_blurb: The Great Lakes of North America — Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie, and Ontario — together hold roughly 20% of the world's fresh surface water. Lake Superior alone is the largest freshwater lake on Earth by surface area. The lakes were scooped out by continental ice sheets during the last ice age; they drain east through the St Lawrence River to the Atlantic. For both the United States and Canada they have been crucial transport, fishing, and industrial waterways for two centuries.

lake-tanganyika.context_blurb: Lake Tanganyika, in the East African Rift Valley, is the second-oldest and second-deepest freshwater lake in the world, after only Lake Baikal in Siberia. It stretches for over 670 kilometres along the border of four African countries — Tanzania, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zambia. Like Baikal, it occupies a long thin crack in a continent that is slowly being pulled apart. Hundreds of species of brightly coloured cichlid fish live in its deep waters, and most of them are found nowhere else.

lake-titicaca.context_blurb: Lake Titicaca straddles the border of Peru and Bolivia high in the Andes Mountains, at over 3,800 metres above sea level. It is the largest freshwater lake in South America by volume and is sometimes called the highest navigable lake in the world. The Uru people live on floating islands built out of totora reeds that grow in the lake. In Andean tradition, the lake is the birthplace of the sun and of the ancestors of the Inca, who stepped out of its waters.

lake-victoria.context_blurb: Lake Victoria is the biggest lake in Africa by surface area and the chief source of the Nile River. It is shared by Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania. The lake is relatively young and shallow for its size. It is also one of the stage-sets of one of the most dramatic recent biological disasters: the introduction of the Nile perch as a food fish in the 1950s and 60s drove hundreds of the lake's distinctive cichlid species to extinction or near-extinction, in what biologists call the largest vertebrate mass extinction of modern times.

laki-1783-the-fissure-that-starved-a-nat.context_blurb: In the summer of 1783 a long volcanic fissure in southern Iceland called Laki opened up and poured out enormous quantities of lava and poisonous sulphur gases for eight months. About a quarter of Iceland's population died in the subsequent famine as livestock perished and crops failed. The gases drifted south across Europe, blanketing it in a strange hazy fog, poisoning crops, and sickening or killing many thousands of people. The disruption may have contributed to the catastrophic grain shortages that helped set the stage for the French Revolution in 1789.

lalibelas-rock-hewn-churches.context_blurb: In the highlands of northern Ethiopia, the medieval king Lalibela ordered an entire cluster of Christian churches carved out of the solid red rock of the mountainside. They were not built up with stones; they were cut down into the earth, each one a single huge sculpture with a hollow interior, roof included. Carved in the 12th and 13th centuries, the churches of Lalibela are still active places of worship for the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, and Christian pilgrims walk between them along passages dug through the rock itself.

lava-lakes-the-worlds-eternal-fire-pits.context_blurb: A persistent lava lake is a pool of molten rock exposed inside a volcanic crater or vent, continuously replenished from below. They are rare — at any given time only a handful exist on Earth. The best-known are at Erta Ale in Ethiopia, Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mount Erebus in Antarctica, and (intermittently) Kilauea in Hawaii. Looking down into one is probably the single most direct window you can get on the molten interior of our planet.

leshan-giant-buddha.context_blurb: At Leshan in Sichuan, China, where three rivers meet, a Chinese Buddhist monk in the 8th century had the mountainside itself carved into a Buddha. The seated figure is more than 70 metres tall from head to foot — the largest ancient stone Buddha in the world. The project took about ninety years. According to tradition, the sculpting was begun to calm the dangerous rapids where the rivers joined, and tons of carved stone dumped into the current from the works really did change its flow.

lhasa-the-potala-palace-above-the-roof-o.context_blurb: Lhasa is the capital of Tibet, high on a plateau at an elevation that leaves most visitors short of breath. Rising above it on a hill is the Potala Palace, a soaring white-and-red fortress-monastery that was for centuries the winter residence of the Dalai Lamas, the spiritual and (until recent times) temporal leaders of Tibetan Buddhism. The current Dalai Lama has lived in exile in India since 1959. The Jokhang Temple down in the old town is the single holiest site in Tibetan Buddhism.

light-bent-into-an-arc-rainbows-and-the-.context_blurb: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends and reflects inside falling raindrops. White sunlight splits into its separate colours and lines up into a circular arc opposite the Sun — red on the outside, violet on the inside, with every observer actually seeing a slightly different rainbow. On rare occasions moonlight is bright enough to produce the same effect, with much paler colours, which is called a moonbow. Double rainbows have a secondary, dimmer bow outside the primary one, with the order of the colours reversed.

lima.context_blurb: Lima, the capital of Peru, lies in a narrow strip of coastal desert between the Pacific Ocean and the foothills of the Andes. It was founded in 1535 by the Spanish conqueror Francisco Pizarro as the seat of Spain's South American viceroyalty, and for about three centuries it was the richest Spanish colonial city on the Pacific coast. It is one of the driest major cities in the world — annual rainfall is almost zero — but it is kept green by rivers running down from the Andes.

linear-b-and-the-burnt-tablets-of-knosso.context_blurb: Linear B is a Bronze Age script found on clay tablets at Knossos on Crete and at several sites on the Greek mainland. For decades after its discovery nobody knew what language it recorded. In the 1950s a brilliant young English architect named Michael Ventris, working with the classicist John Chadwick, finally cracked it: Linear B turned out to be an early form of Greek, written down roughly a thousand years before Homer. The tablets survived precisely because the palaces that stored them burned down, baking the wet clay inventories into permanence.

lisbon-the-quake-that-shook-the-enlighte.context_blurb: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal, perched on seven steep hills above a great natural harbour on the Atlantic. On the morning of November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, a massive earthquake — followed by a tsunami and a city-wide fire — levelled much of it and killed tens of thousands of people. The disaster rattled Europe intellectually, inspiring Voltaire's Candide and provoking fierce arguments about the goodness of God and the natural order. The city was rebuilt afterward on a famously orderly geometric grid in the old lower town.

loess-ice-age-dust-builds-a-plateau.context_blurb: Loess is a fine, pale yellow wind-blown dust that was blown off the barren outwash plains in front of ice-age glaciers and deposited downwind in huge thick blankets. It covers large regions of the central United States, central Europe, Ukraine, and above all northern China, where the Loess Plateau is tens of metres deep in it. Loess is extraordinarily fertile, which is one reason these regions have long been agricultural heartlands. It also erodes dramatically into vertical cliffs and gullies when water cuts into it.

london-the-city-on-the-tidal-thames.context_blurb: London, on the River Thames in southern England, began as a Roman trading post, grew into the capital of medieval England, and in the 18th and 19th centuries became the headquarters of a global empire. The Thames right through central London is tidal, which allowed the Royal Navy's sailing ships to come straight up to the docks. London has repeatedly reinvented itself: a great plague in 1665, a great fire in 1666, bombing in the Blitz of 1940-41, and most recently a transformation from grimy post-industrial port into one of the world's financial centres.

luang-prabang.context_blurb: Luang Prabang is a tiny former royal capital of Laos, tucked at the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan rivers in the mountains of the country's north. Its small centre is packed with gilded Buddhist temples and French-colonial shuttered villas on sleepy lanes, and every morning at dawn barefoot saffron-robed monks walk through the streets in a long procession collecting rice from kneeling residents.

machu-picchu.context_blurb: Machu Picchu is a 15th-century Inca royal estate perched on a ridge in the cloud forest high above the Urubamba River in the Peruvian Andes. It is built of beautifully fitted stone terraces and buildings and is thought to have been constructed for the Inca emperor Pachacuti. The Spanish, remarkably, never found it, which is one reason it survived in better shape than most Inca sites. It was brought to international attention by the American explorer Hiram Bingham III in 1911, who was led there by a local farmer.

madagascar-the-isolated-ark.context_blurb: Madagascar is a huge island off the southeast coast of Africa — bigger than France — that broke off from the African mainland tens of millions of years ago and from the Indian subcontinent soon after. In its long isolation, its plants and animals evolved on their own path. Roughly 90% of the species found on Madagascar live nowhere else on Earth, including all the lemurs, the fossa, and bizarre spiky trees like the baobab and the octopus tree. Humans only arrived about two thousand years ago, which is very recent as islands go.

maelstroms-the-seas-great-whirlpools.context_blurb: A maelstrom is a powerful, often permanent whirlpool caused by strong tidal currents being forced through a narrow strait. The most famous ones are off the Lofoten Islands in northern Norway, where strong Atlantic tides race through gaps between the islands and spin up turbulent eddies big enough to pull small boats around. The word itself is Norwegian. Edgar Allan Poe and Jules Verne both wrote tales about them in which seafarers get sucked down into the depths, but real maelstroms, though impressive, do not actually swallow ships.

manaus.context_blurb: Manaus is the largest city deep inside the Amazon rainforest, in Brazil, far up the Amazon River where it meets the Rio Negro. At the end of the 19th century it exploded into a short-lived rubber boom and was briefly one of the wealthiest cities in the world; the rubber barons built a grand pink opera house in the middle of the jungle, imported European marble and chandeliers, and brought over opera companies from Italy. The boom collapsed when rubber seedlings smuggled to Southeast Asia undercut Brazilian prices.

manila-intramuros.context_blurb: Manila, the capital of the Philippines, was founded by the Spanish in 1571 on the shore of Manila Bay. For some 250 years it anchored the Manila Galleon trade — a yearly convoy of Spanish treasure ships that carried silver and goods between Manila and Acapulco in Mexico, linking Asia into the Spanish global empire. At the heart of old Manila stands Intramuros, the stone-walled Spanish colonial quarter. Most of it was flattened during the Battle of Manila in 1945; portions have been restored, portions remain scarred.

mariachi-jalisco-mexico.context_blurb: Mariachi is the traditional Mexican ensemble music that most of the world now hears as the sound of Mexico. It grew up in the state of Jalisco in western Mexico in the 19th century, out of a blend of indigenous, Spanish, and French musical traditions. A typical mariachi group includes violins, trumpets, Spanish guitars, a round-bellied bass guitar (the guitarron), and a small high-pitched guitar (the vihuela), with the musicians dressed in the ornate charro outfit of the Mexican horseman. Mariachi was added to UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage list in 2011.

marrakech.context_blurb: Marrakech, in Morocco, was founded in 1070 at the foot of the Atlas Mountains and became the royal capital of successive medieval Berber dynasties ruling an empire that reached from Spain to Senegal. Its old medina is enclosed by red-earth walls, from which the city takes its nickname 'the Red City.' At its heart lies the Jemaa el-Fnaa, a huge market square that empties out during the day and fills with storytellers, snake charmers, musicians, and food stalls at dusk.

mecca-and-the-valley-of-the-hijaz.context_blurb: Mecca, in the dry Hijaz region of western Saudi Arabia, is the holiest city of Islam. It is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad in the 6th century and the site of the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine around which Muslim worship is organized. Observant Muslims who can afford to are expected to make the pilgrimage, the Hajj, to Mecca at least once in their lifetime; several million do so every year during a specific week of the Islamic lunar calendar. The city is closed to non-Muslims.

mediterranean-climate-the-scattered-five.context_blurb: A 'Mediterranean climate' means hot dry summers and mild wet winters, and the surprising thing about it is that it occurs in only five places on Earth. One is the actual Mediterranean basin. The other four are coastal California, central Chile, the Cape region of South Africa, and the south and southwest corners of Australia. These five scattered pockets, each sitting on the western edge of a continent at roughly the same latitude, have independently grown drought-tolerant shrublands with similar silver-grey leaves — and in modern times they have become the world's five great wine-making regions.

megathrust-the-deepest-trenches-and-the-.context_blurb: Where one tectonic plate dives down beneath another, the long fault running along the top of the sinking plate is called a megathrust. These are the biggest active faults on Earth, and they produce the biggest earthquakes. The largest earthquakes ever recorded, including the 1960 magnitude 9.5 Chile quake and the 2011 magnitude 9.1 Tohoku quake off Japan, were megathrust events. Earthquakes on megathrusts can also lift the sea floor by metres in seconds, which is what sets off the biggest tsunamis.

meissen-how-europe-cracked-chinas-porcel.context_blurb: For centuries Europeans paid huge sums to import Chinese porcelain, which they could not reproduce. In 1708, in the small Saxon town of Meissen near Dresden in modern Germany, an alchemist named Johann Friedrich Bottger — reportedly working under threat of death from the local prince — finally cracked the recipe. Meissen became the first porcelain factory outside Asia, and its characteristic crossed-swords mark is one of the oldest trademarks still in use. Within a generation, European porcelain workshops had spread across the continent.

melbourne.context_blurb: Melbourne is a southeastern Australian city on a bay off the Southern Ocean.
